docs.title: spieli
docs.text:
A free, interactive map of playgrounds, built from OpenStreetMap data. It shows where playgrounds are, what is on them and who may use them — and, for mappers, what is still missing.

Origin: spieli grew out of the original Berliner Spielplatzkarte by Alex Seidel.

docs.title: See it in action
docs.text:
The public map runs at spieli.eu. Two well-mapped playgrounds in Fulda, both with 360° photos:

  • Carl-Schurz-Straße: 30 play devices, opening hours and operator
  • Galgengraben: 25 play devices and several photos

docs.title: One map, many owners
docs.text: spieli.eu holds no playground data of its own. Each region comes from its own server, a data-node, and visitors' browsers put the regions together on one map. Anyone can run a data-node for their city, district or country and, with it, a map of their own. Why it is built this way: Federation: one map, many owners.

docs.title: Project Overview — spieli
docs.text: spieli is a free, interactive web map for exploring playgrounds based on OpenStreetMap (OSM) data. It is deployable per-region (city, Kreis, Bundesland) by setting two environment variables (OSM_RELATION_ID and PBF_URL). Multiple regional instances can be aggregated into a single federated Hub map. The UI is built in Svelte 5; the data layer is PostgreSQL/PostGIS accessed via PostgREST; everything ships as a Docker Compose stack.

docs.title: Deployment modes
docs.text:
Two orthogonal switches define how the stack runs:

DEPLOY_MODE Services started data-node db + importer + PostgREST (no web UI) ui app (nginx) only, no database data-node-ui full stack (default) APP_MODE Frontend behaviour standalone regional map — fetches from one PostgREST backend hub aggregation map — fetches from all backends in registry.json

The most common configuration is DEPLOY_MODE=data-node-ui + APP_MODE=standalone.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
Geofabrik PBF extract
        │
        ▼
osmium extract (bbox clip)
        │
        ▼
osmium tags-filter (keep playground/tree/pitch/POI tags)
        │
        ▼
osm2pgsql → PostgreSQL tables (planet_osm_point, planet_osm_line, planet_osm_polygon)
        │
        ▼
api.sql → playground_stats materialized view + api schema functions
        │
        ▼
PostgREST → /api/rpc/* HTTP endpoints
        │
        ▼
Browser → tiered orchestrator → OL cluster layer / polygon layer

docs.title: Standalone mode (APP_MODE=standalone)
docs.text:
The default. One region, one database. The tiered orchestrator fires on every moveend:

  • Zoom ≤ 13 → get_playground_clusters(z, bbox) → cluster layer (discs sized by count; with mapping detail on, rings segmented by the complete/partial/missing counts)
  • Zoom > 13 → get_playgrounds_bbox(bbox) → polygon layer (a pin per playground; with mapping detail on, the polygons colour-coded by mapping detail)

Clicking a playground writes #W<osm_id> (or #<slug>/W<osm_id> in hub mode) to the URL hash and opens PlaygroundPanel, which loads equipment, trees, POIs, and reviews.

docs.title: Hub mode (APP_MODE=hub)
docs.text: Aggregates multiple regional data-nodes. The hub orchestrator adds a macro view (zoom ≤ macroMaxZoom, default 7) rendering one ring per backend from get_meta. At higher zooms it fans out to all backends whose bbox intersects the viewport, merges the cluster buckets where their markers would overlap on screen (lib/clusterMerge.js), and renders the union.

docs.title: Using the spieli Map
docs.text:
spieli is a free, interactive playground map based on OpenStreetMap data. This guide explains what you can do with it.

I want to… Go to… Find a playground near me or in a town Finding playgrounds Show only playgrounds with something specific Filters Send someone a link to a playground Sharing a playground Report a playground that is missing Reporting a missing playground

docs.title: Navigating the map
docs.text:
Use your mouse (desktop) or fingers (mobile) to pan and zoom. The map shows:

  • Green circles — at lower zoom levels, nearby playgrounds are grouped into a circle showing how many there are
  • Green pins — zoom in and every playground gets its own pin; a camera on the pin means there is a photo. A grey pin with a lock or a cup tells you who may use it — see Who can use a playground
  • The selected playground's outline — once you open a playground, its area is outlined on the map

This is the default view, made for finding a place to play. If you add data to OpenStreetMap, you can switch on mapping detail instead.

Click or tap any playground to open its detail panel.

docs.title: Finding playgrounds
docs.text:
Search: Type a place name, street, or city into the search box (top bar). The map moves to the matching location.

Suggestions appear once you have typed two characters. You can work the list entirely from the keyboard — ↓ and ↑ move through the suggestions, Enter jumps to the highlighted one (or runs a plain search if none is highlighted), and Esc closes the list without leaving the box — it also cancels a search you have typed but that has not run yet, so the list does not pop back up a moment later. Screen readers announce the list, your position in it, and whether a search is still running.

My location: Tap the location button to centre the map on your current position. Your position is shown as a pulsing blue dot; at high zoom a translucent circle indicates the GPS accuracy. If your browser already allows spieli to see your location, the map centres on you when it opens (unless you opened a link to a playground or a region).

Note: Showing your location only works on a secure (https://) address and with your browser's permission. If the button does nothing, check your browser's location settings.

Region links: Visit a region by name in the URL — e.g. spieli.eu/fulda frames the map on Fulda. spieli looks the name up and shows that area; this works on every spieli map. Share these links like any other address.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Open the filter panel to show only playgrounds that match your needs:

Filter Shows playgrounds that have… Water playground Water play equipment, such as a water pump or a splash pad Baby equipment Equipment suitable for babies Toddler equipment Equipment suitable for toddlers Wheelchair-friendly At least one piece of play equipment tagged wheelchair-accessible — see Wheelchair accessibility Bench At least one bench Picnic table At least one picnic table Shelter A covered shelter Table tennis A table tennis table Football A football pitch Basketball A basketball court Fenced A fence around the playground: recorded on the playground itself, or mapped along at least three quarters of its edge. A fence on one side only (say, towards the road) does not count Dogs allowed Dogs are permitted Themed Has a recognised theme — ship, octopus, castle, … (see Playground themes) With shade Recorded as shaded Lit at night Recorded as lit, all night or at certain times Public only Hide playgrounds that are private or for customers only — see Who can use a playground No private ones Hide only private playgrounds (e.g. a kindergarten's or a school's); customers-only ones stay

Active filters appear as chips below the search bar. Click a chip to remove that filter.

Each filter only finds what has been mapped in OpenStreetMap. Which tags it reads exactly — useful if a playground you know is missing from a filter: OSM Tags spieli Reads.

docs.title: Wheelchair accessibility
docs.text:
This one deserves its own explanation, because it deliberately measures something narrower than the word suggests.

It describes the equipment, not the site. The filter, the map hover icon and the detail panel all answer one question: is there something here a wheelchair-using child can play on? They do not tell you whether the site can be entered or crossed.

That is a deliberate choice. With an accompanying adult, nearly every playground can be entered with a wheelchair, and playgrounds serve roughly ages 0–14 — so the entrance rarely decides anything, while the equipment always does. A playground whose area is tagged as accessible but whose equipment is not will therefore not match this filter.

"Usable with help" counts. Where a piece of equipment is tagged as partially accessible (wheelchair=limited), spieli treats it as suitable. On the objects that actually carry that value — spring riders, seesaws, swings, roundabouts — it means a transfer with assistance, which for this age group is the ordinary way a playground gets used.

A missing badge does not mean "not accessible". The detail panel distinguishes three states, and only two of them are statements:

What you see What it means Wheelchair-friendly Someone tagged at least one device as accessible No wheelchair equipment Someone surveyed the equipment here and none of it is tagged accessible (nothing) Nobody has recorded accessibility for this playground either way — unknown, not negative

The third row is by far the most common. Accessibility tagging is patchy in OpenStreetMap and tends to exist only where a mapper has walked the site with it in mind, so entire regions can show nothing at all. That is a gap in the map, not a finding about the playgrounds.

Please check before relying on it. Everything above reflects what mappers recorded. It is not a substitute for looking at the playground, and "usable with assistance" covers a wide range of ability. If you find a playground tagged wrongly — in either direction — the Edit on MapComplete link in the detail panel opens the playground in an editor.

docs.title: Who can use a playground
docs.text:
Not every playground on the map is open to everyone. spieli reads this from the playground's access tag in OpenStreetMap and shows it the same way on the pin, in the hover preview (desktop) and at the top of the detail panel:

On the map In the panel Meaning Green pin — Public: anyone can play here. Also the case when nothing is recorded Green pin with an amber cup "For customers & guests only" Belongs to a café, a restaurant, a store or a holiday park (access=customers). You can use it while you are a customer there Grey pin with a lock "Private – not open to the public" Belongs to a kindergarten, a school or a residential complex (access=private or access=no). Not open to visitors. Some are usable by a particular group, for example the people living in that housing estate; the panel's details say so when it is recorded

Every playground is shown by default. Two filters hide the ones you can't use:

  • No private ones hides only private playgrounds; café and store playgrounds stay.
  • Public only hides both private and customers-only playgrounds.

Many kindergarten and school playgrounds have no access tag in OpenStreetMap and therefore look public. If you know better, you can add the tag in MapComplete or any OSM editor.

docs.title: Sports pitches outside playgrounds
docs.text:
Enable Sports pitches (outside playgrounds) in the filter panel's Layers section to see sports pitches that are not part of any playground (football fields, basketball courts, skate parks, etc.).

Each pitch gets a white pin with a green rim and a symbol for its sport — football, basketball, tennis, table tennis, volleyball, skating, riding, chess, cycling, archery, athletics, or a generic flag — so pitches are easy to tell apart from the solid green playground pins.

Click or tap a pitch to open its panel — in the same place as a playground's. It shows the pitch's sports and, where they are mapped, its surface, whether it is lit (and when), whether you can just walk in (public, members, fee, booking), opening hours, basketball hoops, wheelchair access, the operator and photos, plus "Take me there", a share link and a link to add missing details in MapComplete. Nothing is shown for what has not been mapped. A shared pitch link looks like …/#P123456 (on the all-regions map …/#region/P123456) and opens the map with the pitch layer switched on. Pitches appear once you zoom in to about the size of a town; when the layer is on but you are zoomed out too far, the filter panel says so.

docs.title: Playground detail panel
docs.text:
Click any playground to open its detail panel. It is ordered by the question you bring to it — is this worth going to with my child? — in three parts, the same on a phone and a computer:

At the top: what decides a visit. You see this without scrolling on a phone.

  • Name, place, the average review rating in stars when there are reviews (only on maps that reach Mangrove through their own server, which is the default), and a lock or cup badge when the playground is private or for customers only (see Who can use a playground). "Take me there" opens navigation (your phone's map app, or OpenStreetMap directions on a computer); Share playground copies a link (see Sharing a playground)
  • Photos — from Wikimedia Commons when the playground links them (tap one for full screen; the author and licence are shown with it), and street-level photos from Panoramax. The street-level viewer opens only when you tap the preview. Without a photo there is one short line with a link to add one
  • Labels for what is recorded, and only then: Babies and Toddlers (equipment suited to them), Shaded / Partly shaded / No shade, Wheelchair-friendly equipment (see Wheelchair accessibility), Fenced and Dogs allowed
  • What kids can do — first the highlights: the playground's theme (see Playground themes), water play, and rare equipment worth a detour (zip line, trampoline, marble run, funnel ball, sledding hill, musical instruments and similar). Below them the activities: swing, slide, rock, climb, balance, spin, bounce, exercise, dig, explore — worked out from the equipment. Five swings are one "swing"; parts of a climbing frame (platforms, ladders) are not counted

When nothing of this is known yet — true for many playgrounds — the panel says so and invites you to add a photo or the details instead.

Further down: the details. The description; Good to know — opening hours, benches, shelters and picnic tables, fitness stations, surface, size and trees, lighting, one line each and only when mapped; Nearby — the nearest toilet, bus stop, ice cream, shop (supermarket, convenience store, bakery), drugstore and emergency care (searched within 5 km by default; the site's operator can change the radius); All equipment, collapsed, with every device and its details; and community reviews from Mangrove.reviews, collapsed until you open them, so nothing is sent to Mangrove before that (including reviews written in MapComplete or on mangrove.reviews).

At the bottom: background. The operator and contact details, how old the map data is, and Edit on MapComplete to add or improve information in OpenStreetMap.

To close the panel, use its close or "back to map" button — or your browser's back: on a phone the back swipe takes you from the panel back to the map instead of leaving spieli.

docs.title: Playground themes
docs.text:
Some playgrounds have a theme — they are built around a motif like a ship, castle, or octopus. When OpenStreetMap records a theme for a playground, spieli highlights it in the detail panel:

  • First among the Highlights near the top: "Ship-themed playground" when the whole playground is themed, or the theme's name when only some equipment is.
  • A symbol beside individual pieces of equipment in the equipment list, for themed devices.

To keep the highlight meaningful, spieli only shows a curated set of recognised whole-playground themes: ship, castle, spider web, water, adventure, rocket, dragon, octopus, and circus. Common animal spring-rider shapes (a horse or duck rocker) are not treated as playground themes, since almost any spring rider can take one of those shapes.

Themes come straight from the playground:theme tag in OpenStreetMap — you can add or correct one via Edit on MapComplete in the panel. Themes are shown only in the detail panel, not on the map.

docs.title: Sharing a playground
docs.text: Each playground has a unique URL. When you open a playground, the address in your browser changes to end in something like #W37808214. Share that URL, or use Share playground in the panel, to link directly to a specific playground. A sports pitch's link uses P instead (#P123456). On the all-regions map the link also names the region, e.g. #hessen/W37808214.

docs.title: The all-regions map
docs.text:
spieli.eu combines many regional maps into one. Each region comes from its own server (why: Federation: one map, many owners). Most things work exactly as on a single region's map; a few are added:

  • One circle per region when zoomed far out. Its number is the region's playground count. Tap it to zoom into that region; for a region that is offline or has no data, a short note opens instead. Zoom in further and the circles give way to the usual playground circles and pins.
  • A circle can look different when a region is not answering normally. The label tells you why: offline (the region's server cannot be reached; the number is the last one known), updating (it is importing fresh data), no data (it answers but has no playgrounds yet). With a filter active, no match means none of its playgrounds fit the filter, and unfiltered means the region cannot apply your filter (for example because it runs an older version), so all of its playgrounds are counted.
  • "Filter covers N of M regions" appears at that zoom level when some regions could not apply your filter.
  • The region list. The button at the bottom left with the number of regions and playgrounds opens a list of all regions, with each one's playground count, how old its data is, and whether it is reachable or updating, and links to its imprint and privacy policy. Regions outside Germany carry a country code such as SK; screen readers announce the full country name.
  • Links name the region. A shared playground link looks like …/#hessen/W37808214.

If one region is offline, every other region keeps working.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
spieli shows its buttons and texts in German, English or Slovak, following your browser's language; any other browser language gets English. A site can also be set to one language by whoever runs it. There is no switch in the map itself.

Playground names and other details come from OpenStreetMap and are shown as mapped, usually in the local language.

More languages are being translated on Weblate, and help there is welcome.

docs.title: Installing spieli as an app
docs.text:
On a phone, spieli can sit on your home screen like an app: one tap opens the map full-screen, without the browser's address bar.

  • iPhone / iPad (Safari): the share button → Add to Home Screen.
  • Android (Chrome): Install as app in the About dialog (the ⓘ button), or the browser menu → Install app.
  • Android (Firefox): menu → Install (or Add to Home screen).

Each spieli region installs as its own app, under its own name — the Fulda map and the all-Germany hub can sit side by side.

On a desktop, Chrome and Edge (install icon in the address bar) and Safari on a Mac (File → Add to Dock) can do the same; Firefox on the desktop cannot (only an experimental "Taskbar Tabs" feature on Windows).

docs.title: Keyboard and screen readers
docs.text:
While a dialog or a full-screen photo is open, the keyboard stays with it: focus moves into it, Tab cycles through its own controls only — not the map, the search or the buttons hidden behind it — and screen readers read only the dialog. Close it with Esc or its close button, and focus returns to where you were.

The search box can be used entirely from the keyboard, see Finding playgrounds.

docs.title: About, imprint and privacy
docs.text: The ⓘ button opens the About dialog: where the data comes from and how to add to it, the offer to report a missing playground, Install as app where your browser supports it, links to the source code and to translating spieli, and Imprint and Privacy policy for the site you are on, when its operator has provided them. The imprint names whoever runs this map. On the all-regions map, each region's own imprint and privacy policy are linked from the region list.

docs.title: When the background map goes blank
docs.text: Some sites use a background map that only has detail for certain countries. If you move the map outside that area, the background turns plain and a note says No detailed map data for this area. Playgrounds are still shown where the site has them.

docs.title: Reporting a missing playground
docs.text:
Know a playground that is not on the map? Press the green map pin with a plus at the bottom right, below the zoom buttons. You can also use the offer that appears when a search finds nothing or when no playgrounds are in view, or open it from the About dialog. The back button or gesture closes the report again.

  1. Mark the spot. Move the map until the cross sits on the playground. If your location is known, "I'm standing in front of it" jumps there. If a known playground is right next to the spot, spieli asks whether you mean that one. Outside the area this map has data for, spieli cannot check that, so it only offers MapComplete, which shows what OpenStreetMap already has there.
  2. Choose how to report it:
    • Leave a hint — no account needed. Tick what is there (swings, slide, …), add a name or a note if you like, and send. The hint becomes a public OpenStreetMap note that local mappers review and use to add the playground. The OpenStreetMap Foundation stores your IP address with the note to prevent abuse; notes are public and you cannot delete them yourself afterwards, so don't include personal details.
    • Add it yourself in MapComplete, with a free OpenStreetMap account.
  3. Follow up. If you tick "Remember this hint on this device" before sending, the hint shows up on your map as a small pin (in this browser only). Tap it to see whether a mapper has dealt with it yet. Without the tick, nothing is stored.

Nothing is sent until you press Send hint; opening or moving the map never contacts OpenStreetMap's notes service.

docs.title: Telling us what is at a playground
docs.text:
Been to a playground the map knows little about? Open it and tap Tell us what is there in the panel, or Something missing? Send a hint right under "What kids can do" in any playground's panel.

A short form opens over the panel. It offers only what the map does not know yet: equipment (swing, slide, sandpit, climbing frame, …), whether it is fenced, whether there is shade, and a name if it has none. Add a note if you like and press Send hint. Like a missing-playground report, the hint becomes a public OpenStreetMap note at the playground, with a link to it and the matching tags, so local mappers can add it quickly. No account is needed; the same notice about what the OpenStreetMap Foundation stores applies, and together with missing-playground reports you can send three per visit. The back button or gesture, or Escape, closes the form and leaves the panel open.

docs.title: Adding or improving data
docs.text:
All playground data comes from OpenStreetMap. If a playground is missing (see above), has the wrong location, or lacks details:

  1. Click the playground and open its detail panel
  2. Use Edit on MapComplete to open MapComplete — a beginner-friendly OSM editor focused on playgrounds
  3. Or edit directly at openstreetmap.org

Changes you make in OpenStreetMap appear in spieli after the next data import. How often that runs is up to whoever runs the map, typically every few days; see Data age.

The About dialog (the ⓘ button) has the same links in one place: MapComplete, the OpenStreetMap wiki, and the local mapping chat where the site names one.

docs.title: Data age
docs.text:
A playground's panel shows Data as of: … ago: how old the OpenStreetMap snapshot is that the map was built from. Tap it for an explanation. An edit you make in OpenStreetMap shows up only once a newer snapshot has been imported. How often that happens depends on the map: imports usually run every few days, and the snapshot itself can be a day or so older than the import.

On the all-regions map, the region list shows the same age per region ("OSM data: … old").

docs.title: Mapping detail colours
docs.text:
Mapping detail is off by default. Switch it on with the bar-chart button next to the info and filter buttons (on phones and desktop alike) and turn on Show mapping detail. The map then shows each playground's area, colour-coded by how much of it has been mapped in OpenStreetMap, and the circles split into coloured segments:

Colour What it means Light green Detailed — mapped play equipment and at least one detail (surface, opening hours, or access) Dark green Basic — one of the two, not both Slate grey No details yet — the playground exists in OSM but carries no equipment and no details

With mapping detail on, the playground panel shows a small tool block right under its title: the playground's mapping-detail badge and the Edit in MapComplete link. The rest of the panel stays in the same order. With mapping detail off, the block is not there and the MapComplete link is at the bottom of the panel.

Your choice is remembered in this browser. To send someone a link that opens with mapping detail on — say, to a fellow mapper — add ?detail=1 to the address (for example …/fulda?detail=1), or use the share button on a playground while mapping detail is on: the link it copies includes it. Opening such a link does not change the other person's own setting; ?detail=0 does the opposite.

Play equipment means slides, swings, climbing frames and the like, plus ball courts. A bench or picnic table on its own does not make a playground "basic" — those are useful to know about, but they say nothing about whether there is anything to play on.

With mapping detail on, a playground's panel also says under its badge what is missing for the next step — for example "Not mapped yet: the play equipment". The MapComplete link next to the badge opens this playground to add it. Detailed playgrounds get no hint.

A camera glyph marks playgrounds that also have a photo. Photos are a bonus, not part of mapping detail — a playground with everything mapped except a picture still counts as detailed.

The colours describe the OSM data, not the real-world quality of the playground. The lowest step means nobody has mapped it yet, which is an invitation to help rather than a warning.

docs.title: Showing only some states
docs.text:
The mapping-detail button (not the filter panel) lets you show or hide playgrounds by how much of them is mapped:

State Meaning detailed (light green) Mapped play equipment and at least one detail (surface, opening hours, or access) basic (dark green) One of the two, not both no details yet (slate grey) Neither

All three states are shown by default. Deactivate a state to hide those playgrounds — for example, uncheck no details yet and basic to see only well-documented playgrounds, or uncheck detailed and basic to find playgrounds still needing OSM survey work.

These choices only apply while mapping detail is switched on. Switch it off and every playground is shown again; switch it back on and your choices return.

docs.title: Print a poster
docs.text:
There is a poster for hanging up locally, at a kindergarten, a café or a playground noticeboard: a pixel-art scene and a QR code to spieli.eu, in German, English and Slovak. The print-ready files are in the repository under marketing/poster/print/:

  • poster-<lang>-a4.pdf — one poster on an A4 page
  • poster-<lang>-2up-a4.pdf — two posters on A4 landscape with cut marks, for handing out
  • poster-<lang>.png — for use online

Print at actual size / 100 %, not "fit to page", and scan the QR code off the printout before hanging it up. (Changing or rebuilding it: Build the Poster.)

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
• No user accounts, no analytics, no cookies. A few settings are kept in your browser itself (for example whether mapping detail is on).
  • By default your browser only talks to the spieli site you opened. Search, the background map, photos and reviews are fetched by that server for you, so those services never see your address.
  • The exceptions: street-level photo thumbnails (and the viewer, once you open it) come from Panoramax directly, and a "Missing a playground?" hint goes to OpenStreetMap when you send it.
  • The server keeps no log of what you look at or search for.

How and why: Privacy by design. The full list of services: External Services.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Share OpenSpec specs and archive in git
docs.text:
• Status: Revised (see ## Revision 2026-04-20 below)
  • Date: 2026-04-19
  • Deciders: @mfuhrmann

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We use OpenSpec as an AI-assisted spec/change workflow alongside Claude Code. It writes three things to openspec/ in the repo root:

Path Contents Lifecycle openspec/specs/<capability>/spec.md Durable per-capability requirements Long-lived, updated when requirements change openspec/changes/<name>/ In-flight change proposals (proposal, design, tasks, deltas) Short-lived — created, worked on, archived openspec/changes/archive/<date>-<name>/ Frozen record of a shipped change Long-lived, append-only

Today .gitignore contains a single line:

openspec/

That made sense while we were the only user of the tool, but the repo has since accumulated enough OpenSpec state that the wholesale ignore costs more than it saves:

  • 7 capability specs live only on one laptop. The knowledge they capture (deployment-mode-selection, hub-ui-parity, mkdocs-site, playwright-ci, rc-container-tag, scheduled-importer, slim-readme) is already reflected in shipped code and docs, but the why behind each requirement is locked up.
  • 6 archived change decisions (proposal + design + tasks for each shipped change) record the trade-offs we walked through. None of that survives in git history — commit messages capture what shipped, not why we rejected the alternatives.
  • We can't hand off an OpenSpec-driven task to a collaborator via a PR. Issue [#190] worked around this by pasting the design inline into the issue body, which is fragile.
  • Claude Code can't read prior design decisions on a fresh clone, which defeats the point of writing them down.

A second contributor (@ronnytrommer) also uses Claude Code + OpenSpec, so the tool is no longer single-operator.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Track openspec/specs/ and openspec/changes/archive/ in git. Keep active openspec/changes/<name>/ directories ignored.

Replace the openspec/ line in .gitignore with:

# OpenSpec — track specs + archived decisions, hide in-flight changes
openspec/changes/*/
!openspec/changes/archive/
!openspec/changes/archive/**

This gives us:

Path Tracked? Why openspec/specs/** yes Durable requirements; AI tools benefit from reading them on a fresh clone openspec/changes/archive/** yes Decision log — the "why" that commit messages don't carry openspec/changes/<active>/** no In-flight, churny, often private-in-progress thinking openspec/AGENTS.md, top-level config yes So clones know what the directory is for

An openspec/README.md pointing at this ADR goes in as part of the implementation so a confused first-time reader has a landing.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• P0 — Keep openspec/ wholesale ignored. The current state. Cheap to maintain but makes every decision a single-laptop secret.
  • P1 — Track openspec/specs/ only. Gets the durable requirements into git but loses the decision log — the most expensive thing to recreate. Rejected.
  • P3 — Track everything under openspec/. Includes in-flight changes. Creates noisy diffs on every exploration session and forces "is my WIP proposal ready for a teammate to see?" into a constant judgment call. Rejected.

P2 (this ADR) is the sweet spot: tracks the two artifact kinds with long-term value, leaves working-memory unshared.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Specs and archived decisions survive across machines and appear in fresh clones.
  • A collaborator can take over an issue and, after the change is archived, the decision rationale ships with the merge.
  • Claude Code (or any AI tool) can read openspec/specs/ and prior archives as grounding context.
  • Git history becomes the AI memory multiplier — every future session inherits the reasoning of past sessions.

Negative / to manage:

  • First-time coordination gotcha. @ronnytrommer has a local openspec/ with specs and archives that diverge from @mfuhrmann's. When we commit the baseline, one of us will have a messy first pull. Two options:
  • Option A (default): @mfuhrmann lands the baseline. @ronnytrommer reviews the diff against his local state, rebases any genuine differences onto the shared baseline in a follow-up PR.
  • Option B: pre-sync by diffing the two openspec/specs/ trees before committing. More work, smaller follow-up.
  • In-flight proposals are no longer on the teammate's radar by default. For handoff we'll keep using GitHub issues with the proposal pasted inline (pattern established by issue #190). If this becomes a real friction we can revisit.
  • openspec validate must stay green on main. Add it to CI as part of the implementation so broken archives don't rot the shared history.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text:
Tracked in issue [#193]. Summary:

  1. .gitignore: replace the openspec/ line with the pattern in "Decision" above.
  2. Baseline commit: add openspec/specs/, openspec/changes/archive/, openspec/AGENTS.md, openspec/project.md, and a small openspec/README.md pointing at this ADR.
  3. .claude/CLAUDE.md (or project CLAUDE.md): note that archived changes and specs are now tracked, so Claude can read them; active changes remain local.
  4. Coordinate the baseline with @ronnytrommer using Option A above, unless Option B is obviously cheaper by then.
  5. Optional follow-up: add openspec validate to CI.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• OpenSpec
  • Issue [#190] — handoff workaround that motivated this ADR
  • Issue [#193] — implementation

docs.title: Revision 2026-04-20
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (supersedes the original Decision above)
  • Deciders: @mfuhrmann, @ronnytrommer

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text: The "real friction" scenario anticipated in Negative / to manage above has fired sooner than expected. During a collaborative /opsx:explore session, @ronnytrommer drafted two multi-file change proposals (add-tiered-playground-delivery, add-federated-playground-clustering) that each span four files: proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md, and a nested specs/<capability>/spec.md. The original ADR's prescribed handoff — paste the proposal inline into a GitHub issue (pattern from

docs.title: 190) — does not scale to multi-file proposals: eight files pasted into
docs.text:
one issue body is unreadable, and round-tripping edits between issue comments and local openspec/changes/ diverges almost immediately.

Waiting to see whether this pattern recurs before revisiting would create the same single-laptop-knowledge problem the original ADR was written to fix, just one level down.

docs.title: Revised decision
docs.text:
Track the whole openspec/ tree in git, including active openspec/changes/<name>/ directories. Replace the selective pattern with a simple removal of the openspec/ line from .gitignore.

Path Tracked? Change from original openspec/specs/** yes unchanged openspec/changes/archive/** yes unchanged openspec/changes/<active>/** yes new — was excluded openspec/config.yaml, openspec/AGENTS.md, top-level yes unchanged

docs.title: Consequences of the revision
docs.text:
Positive (additive to the original Consequences):

  • Multi-file proposals can be handed off via ordinary branch + PR workflow, not issue-paste.
  • Every commit that touches a proposal surfaces in normal code-review tooling.
  • Claude Code agents on any account read the same active-proposal set on a fresh clone.

Accepted costs:

  • Noisy diffs on every exploration session. Mitigated by branch discipline: exploratory thinking stays on an unpushed local branch until it is "worth showing." Only merge to main when a proposal is ready for collaboration or ready to implement.
  • "Is my WIP ready for a teammate?" as a constant judgment call. Resolved by the same branch discipline. Local branch = private thinking; pushed branch / draft PR = ready for collaboration; main = shared baseline.
  • Active-change churn in main history. Accepted. Use draft PRs for in-progress proposals so the history of the proposal is legible (one PR per proposal is the default; multiple commits within the PR are fine).

docs.title: Coordination for the baseline commit
docs.text:
Both contributors already have local openspec/ directories that diverge (see original Negative / to manage). The original ADR proposed Option A (one contributor lands the baseline, the other rebases) with @mfuhrmann as the default baseliner.

Under this revision the baseline includes active proposals too, which amplifies the divergence risk. We switch to a coordinated baseline:

  1. @ronnytrommer opens a PR containing: (a) this ADR revision, (b) the .gitignore change, (c) his local openspec/ tree.
  2. @mfuhrmann reviews the PR, resolves any conflict with his own local tree in review (if his active proposals differ from what @ronnytrommer has captured, he commits the authoritative versions onto the PR branch before merge).
  3. On merge, both contributors hard-reset their local openspec/ to the committed tree, then cherry-pick any diverged local commits back on top.

docs.title: When to revert
docs.text: If the branch-discipline cost outlives the collaboration benefit, revert by restoring the .gitignore pattern from the original Decision and going back to issue-paste handoff. The original Decision remains available verbatim above this revision block.

docs.title: Federation: one map, many owners
docs.text:
spieli.eu shows playgrounds across Germany on one map. The map itself, the hub, holds none of them.

Every region comes from its own server, a data-node. The hub is little more than a list of those servers. When you open the map, your browser asks the data-nodes for the region you are looking at and puts the answers together on screen. Who runs a data-node, and where, makes no difference to the map: any server that speaks the same API can be on the list.

This page explains why spieli is built that way, and what follows from it. If you want to set one up, go to Host a Region or Federated Deployment instead.

docs.title: The picture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    hub["hub (spieli.eu)<br/>app + a list of data-node addresses"]
    browser["your browser"]
    subgraph nodes["data-nodes"]
        hessen["Hessen"]
        bayern["Bayern"]
        yours["your region<br/>(+ own map)"]
    end
    osm["OpenStreetMap<br/>re-imported every few days"]

    hub -- "1. who covers what?" --> browser
    browser -- "2. only the regions you are looking at" --> hessen
    browser --> bayern
    browser --> yours
    osm --> hessen
    osm --> bayern
    osm --> yours

docs.title: The hub owns nothing
docs.text:
The hub has no database. Its whole knowledge of the world is a registry.json: a name, an address and a short slug per region. Everything you see on the map is fetched live from the region that holds it.

That means there is no central copy of the data to keep in sync, to back up, or to lose. Moving a region to another server, or to another operator, means changing one address in that list.

docs.title: Every region belongs to whoever runs it
docs.text: A data-node is run by someone who cares about that region: a local OpenStreetMap group, a municipality, a family association, or one person with a small server. They choose the boundary, they decide when to join, and they can leave again. Their server, their imprint, their responsibility for exactly their own part, nothing more.

docs.title: Joining gives you something, rather than taking something
docs.text: A data-node can also serve its own map under its own name (data-node-ui). Someone covering Austria could run my-playground-map.at for people there and appear on spieli.eu at the same time, from the same server and the same data. Taking part in the shared map does not mean giving up your own.

docs.title: Start small, grow from below
docs.text: A region does not have to be a country. A state, a district or a single city is enough, and neighbours can add the areas around it later. A small VPS carries even a large state; the import is the only demanding moment. Measured figures: Sizing.

docs.title: One program, different roles
docs.text: There is no separate "hub software" and "node software". Hub, data-node and a stand-alone regional map are the same spieli release with a different setting (DEPLOY_MODE, APP_MODE). Anything new in spieli reaches every role with the same upgrade, and anyone who can run one part can run all of them. See Deployment modes.

docs.title: A failure stays local
docs.text:
If one data-node goes down, only its region is missing. The hub draws it as an offline ring and every other region keeps working. The same goes for a region that is in the middle of a re-import: it shows as updating instead of disappearing. See Federation reference → Ring states.

This holds per data-node, not per machine: data-nodes that share a server also share its outages.

docs.title: It stays fast however many regions join
docs.text: Your browser only asks the data-nodes whose area overlaps what you are looking at. A view of Berlin sends no request to a server covering Bavaria. Zoomed out to the whole country, the map draws one ring per region from numbers it already has, and asks the data-nodes only while a filter is active. Answers are drawn as they arrive, so a slow region never holds up a fast one. See How the hub works internally.

docs.title: The data is OpenStreetMap's, not ours
docs.text: No data-node invents or edits anything. Each one re-imports its region from OpenStreetMap every few days. So the way to make the map better is to improve OpenStreetMap, and every improvement reaches every map built on it, not only spieli. Federation spreads the work of serving the data; the data itself stays common property.

docs.title: Privacy follows the same split
docs.text: Once regions are run by different people, no single operator sees every region a visitor looks at. See Privacy by design.

docs.title: How it runs today
docs.text:
Honestly: spieli.eu is still mostly one person's server. At the time of writing, the hub and 15 German states run side by side as separate stacks on one VPS, operated by the project maintainer, with room left for the one re-import that runs at a time (Sizing → Several regions on one host). The federation is real in the software, not yet in who runs it.

That is a starting point, not the plan. Each state is already its own data-node with its own database and address, so handing one over to someone else, or adding a region from somewhere else, needs no change to spieli at all. That is what Host a Region is for.

docs.title: What this asks of you
docs.text:
Federation is not free of cost. It moves work outward:

  • Someone has to run each region. A region nobody hosts stays empty on the map, which is why we are looking for hosts.
  • Each data-node is a public server. It needs HTTPS, updates and, in Germany, an imprint. The installer and automatic updates keep this small, but it is not zero.
  • Regions should not overlap. Two data-nodes covering the same area would show the same playgrounds twice. The hub drops exact duplicates and warns when one region lies entirely inside another (a partial overlap goes unflagged), but choosing boundaries is a matter of talking to each other, in #spieli:matrix.org.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: I want to… Go to… Put my region on spieli.eu Host a Region Run my own hub with several regions Federated Deployment Run many regions on one server Single-host Federation Know exactly how the hub talks to data-nodes Federation reference

docs.title: Privacy by design
docs.text:
A playground map is used by parents, often on a phone, often near home. Which playgrounds someone looks at, and where they search, says a lot about where their children are. spieli is built so that this information goes as few places as possible, and so that the places it does go are named.

This page explains the approach. The service-by-service detail is in External Services.

docs.title: One address instead of many
docs.text:
A typical web map loads its background tiles from a tile provider, its search from a geocoder, its photos from a photo host and its reviews from a review service. Each of them receives the visitor's IP address and learns what that visitor is looking at.

In a default spieli deployment, the browser talks to one server: the spieli instance it opened (on a hub, also the servers of the regions on screen, see below). That instance fetches everything else on the visitor's behalf and keeps a cache:

flowchart LR
    browser["your browser"]
    instance["spieli instance<br/>app · API · cache"]
    services["background map<br/>search (Nominatim)<br/>photos (Wikimedia Commons)<br/>reviews (Mangrove)"]

    browser -- "the only connection" --> instance
    instance -- "fetches on your behalf,<br/>without your address" --> services

The outbound requests carry no cookies, no referrer, no browser language and no forwarded IP address. The services see a spieli server, not a visitor. And many visitors share one cached answer: the background map of Fulda is fetched once, not once per family.

If a service cannot be reached, the feature fails instead of quietly falling back to a direct connection. A fallback would reveal exactly the addresses the proxy is there to protect, at the moment nobody is watching.

docs.title: Nothing is written down
docs.text:
The server keeps no access log at all, not for the map, not for the API, not for the proxied services. Proxying moves the visitor's request stream onto the operator's server, and recording it there would create the very trail the proxy removes. Only errors are logged. An operator who puts their own reverse proxy in front of spieli has to make sure it does not log those requests one layer up.

spieli sets no cookies, runs no analytics and has no user accounts.

docs.title: What still leaves, and when
docs.text:
Three things still connect the browser to a third party. Each is deliberate, and each happens only in a specific situation:

What When Why it is not proxied Panoramax street-level photo thumbnails When you open a playground that has street-level photos The photo service redirects to hosts that change per installation; a proxy cannot follow them The Panoramax viewer Only when you click the thumbnail to open it, and only until you close it It is a full application from another site; running it under spieli's address would hand it spieli's privileges An OpenStreetMap note ("Missing a playground?") Only when you press Send, and a sent hint's status only when you tap its pin Sent through one server, every anonymous note would come from one address, which is what OpenStreetMap's spam protection blocks

The viewer goes furthest of the three, which is why it waits for a click. An iframe gets its own browsing context on the provider's site, with cookies, storage and the provider's own scripts; the live viewer tries to set an analytics cookie. spieli loads it with referrerpolicy="no-referrer" and a sandbox, but the sandbox has to allow scripts and the frame's own origin, or the viewer renders nothing, so it does not stop that cookie. What protects visitors is that the iframe does not exist until they ask for it, and is destroyed again when they close it.

Links to MapComplete, OpenStreetMap or Wikidata transfer nothing until they are clicked.

Panel sections that start closed contact nothing until they are opened. Reviews start closed.

docs.title: What stays in your browser
docs.text:
spieli stores a few things in the browser itself. None of them is sent anywhere:

What Why When Whether mapping detail is on So the map looks the same next time When you switch it Number of hints sent in this session Limits hints to three per session When you send one; cleared when the tab closes Your sent hints, to show their status So you can see whether someone added the playground Only if you tick the box to keep them; off by default A key pair for reviews It is your identity to Mangrove, so your reviews can be signed Only when you write your first review

docs.title: Federation keeps it split
docs.text: In a federation, the browser fetches each region's playgrounds from that region's own server. Once regions are run by different people, no single operator sees every region a visitor looks at. Data-nodes have no accounts and no cookies, nobody can write anything through them, and by default they log nothing either.

docs.title: The operator decides, and the privacy page follows
docs.text:
An operator can switch any proxy off, or use a third-party background map instead of the cached one. That is a legitimate choice, but it is never silent: the instance generates its privacy page and its Content Security Policy from the same configuration, so a service that is contacted directly is also named on the privacy page and allowed in the policy. Neither is hard-coded.

That is also why we do not write that spieli "does not track anyone". What a given instance does depends on how it is configured. What spieli guarantees is that the default is as quiet as we could make it, and that every deviation from it shows up where visitors can read it.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: I want to… Go to… See every external service and how it is reached External Services Switch a proxy off, or size the cache Basemap and external services → External-service proxies Understand the Content Security Policy Security → nginx security headers Write the imprint and privacy notice for my instance Configure the instance → Legal pages

docs.title: Add a Playground Device
docs.text: Every playground device that OSM records — slides, swings, climbing frames, balance beams — is defined in one place: app/src/lib/objPlaygroundEquipment.js. Adding support for a new device type is a small, self-contained change.

docs.title: Step 1 — Find the OSM tag
docs.text:
OSM uses the tag playground=<value> to describe individual devices. The full list of documented values is at wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:playground.

For example, a balance beam is playground=balance_beam.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add an entry to objDevices
docs.text:
Open app/src/lib/objPlaygroundEquipment.js and add a new key to the objDevices object. Copy an existing entry as a template:

balance_beam: {
    name_de: "Balancierbalken",
    image: "File:Playground balance beam.jpg",
    category: "balance",
},

Field reference:

Field Required Description name_de Yes German name. A last resort: a missing translation falls back to English first (svelte-i18n's fallbackLocale), and only a key missing in English too shows name_de image No Commons (or OSM wiki) File: title for an example illustration (see Step 4). Omit if no good image exists. category Yes Decides the device's symbol in the equipment list and on the map. One of stationary, structure_parts, swing, balance, climbing, rotating, sand, water, activity, motion, topographical, other — see Equipment Types.

Some older entries also carry filterable and filter_attr. The current app does not read them; leave them out.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add the display name
docs.text:
The panel shows equipment.devices.<key> from the locale files; a locale without the key shows the English one, and name_de appears only if English lacks it too. Add the key to locales/en.json and locales/de.json in the same commit (no other locale file by hand — see Translation Workflow):

"devices": {
    …
    "balance_beam": "Balance beam"
}

docs.title: Step 4 — Find an illustration
docs.text:
1. Search commons.wikimedia.org for the device name in English.
  2. Pick a clear, representative photo and copy its filename — it starts with File: (e.g. File:Playground balance beam.jpg).
  3. Paste it as the image value.

  4. Resolve it to a real file URL and commit the result with your change:

    make equipment-images     # rewrites app/src/lib/equipmentImages.generated.json

    The app serves illustrations from that generated file, through its own /ext/wikimedia/ proxy, so without this step the image does not show. A name that resolves on neither Commons nor the OSM wiki fails the target. Details: Update Generated Assets → Equipment illustrations.

If you can't find a suitable image, omit the image field. No broken icon will appear.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
make dev

Open the app at http://localhost:5173, navigate to a playground that has the device, and expand its entry in the equipment list. You should see the name in the current language, the example image, and any attributes.

Finding a playground with a specific device

Use Overpass Turbo — search for playground=balance_beam (replace with your tag value) to locate playgrounds that have it mapped.

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text: Branch, commit and open the pull request as described in Local Development → Start here. The change touches app/src/lib/objPlaygroundEquipment.js, app/src/lib/equipmentImages.generated.json, locales/en.json and locales/de.json.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Equipment Types: every device spieli already knows
  • Update Generated Assets → Equipment illustrations

docs.title: Add a Filter
docs.text: How to add a filter to the filter panel, from the database flag to the removable chip. There are two kinds: a standard filter (off by default, narrows the map to playgrounds that have something) and a visibility filter (on by default, hides a category when switched off). How filter state flows through the frontend: Frontend Guide → Filter flow.

docs.title: Standard boolean filter (default off)
docs.text:
Most filters default to false (inactive). Enabling one restricts the map to playgrounds that have the feature. Example: water playground filter.

1. importer/api.sql: the flag — add a boolean column to playground_stats (the equip_stats CTE computes the existing ones from the equipment inside each playground) and run make db-apply. A full make import is only needed if the flag depends on a tag the tag filter does not keep yet. Which tags set the existing flags: OSM Tags spieli Reads → Filters.

2. app/src/stores/filters.js — add the key to defaultFilters and add match logic to matchesFilters():

export const defaultFilters = {
    …
    myNewFilter: false,
};

// in matchesFilters():
if (filters.myNewFilter && !props.my_flag) return false;

3. app/src/lib/api.js — add the cluster-tier RPC param to clusterFilterMap:

const clusterFilterMap = {
    …
    myNewFilter: 'filter_my_new',
};

4. importer/api.sql: the RPC parameter — add a parameter to get_playground_clusters() (default false) and a WHERE clause. Also drop the old function signature and update the GRANT. Run make db-apply to apply.

5. app/src/components/FilterPanel.svelte — add the icon to FILTER_ICONS, and the label's translation key to locales/en.json and locales/de.json only — the other locale files belong to Weblate (Translation Workflow).

6. app/src/components/FilterChips.svelte — add the key to FILTER_KEYS. Don't skip this. The chip bar is the only way to clear an active filter from outside the panel; a filter missing from FILTER_KEYS can be set but shows no removable chip. FILTER_KEYS must stay in sync with the boolean filters in defaultFilters (excluding the standalonePitches layer toggle and the show* completeness states, which are not chip-rendered).

7. Unit tests — add cases to app/src/stores/filters.test.js.

docs.title: Visibility filter (default on)
docs.text:
Use this pattern when users toggle which categories to show rather than requiring a feature. Example: the completeness filter (showComplete/showPartial/showMissing).

Rule: anything that affects what is fetched or drawn reads effectiveFilterStore, never filterStore. The completeness states are only in force while mapping detail is on (#924); effectiveFilterStore forces them to true otherwise, and it also emits when mapping detail is toggled, so subscribers refetch. Only the controls that edit filters read filterStore.

Key differences from the standard pattern:

  • Default value is true (show all); deactivating hides a category.
  • matchesFilters() checks the prop and returns false to hide.
  • hasActiveFilters() detects activity via !filters.myVisibilityKey.
  • activeFilterCount() increments when false, not true.
  • Each popover resets only its own keys: FilterPanel's and FilterChips' "clear all" leave the completeness states alone, and MappingDetailControl resets only those.
  • Cluster RPC params default true; pass 'false' only when deactivated:
// api.js — in fetchPlaygroundClusters:
if (filters.showMyCategory === false) params.set('filter_my_category', 'false');
  • SQL param defaults true; add a WHERE clause that ORs across all enabled states:
AND (
  (ps.my_col = 'a' AND filter_a)
  OR (ps.my_col = 'b' AND filter_b)
)

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Run make test-unit, then import a region that has playgrounds with the feature and check that the filter narrows both tiers (zoomed out and zoomed in) and shows a chip you can remove. In a hub, a backend on an older release cannot apply the new parameter; the hub then shows it as unfiltered (Ring states).

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text: Branch, commit and open the pull request as described in Local Development → Start here. Tag it requires-schema-update, since api.sql changed.

docs.title: Add a POI Category
docs.text: Nearby POIs (toilets, shops, bus stops, etc.) are shown in the playground detail panel. To add or remove a category, touch three code files and the two source locale files:

docs.title: Step 1 — Importer: importer/import.sh → osmium tags-filter
docs.text:
The osmium tags-filter allowlist controls which OSM tags survive the pre-import clip. If a tag is not listed here, nodes/ways carrying it are dropped before osm2pgsql loads them and the database never sees them.

Add or remove entries for both nodes (n/) and ways (w/):

The list is TAG_FILTERS; nodes and ways have separate blocks:

n/shop=bakery
…
w/shop=bakery

After editing, a full re-import is required (make import). Tag the PR with requires-reimport.

docs.title: Step 2 — Database: importer/api.sql → get_pois()
docs.text:
The pois_point and pois_polygon CTEs filter OSM nodes and polygons by tag. Add or remove entries from the WHERE clause in both CTEs:

-- in both CTEs, pois_point and pois_polygon
OR p.shop IN ('chemist', 'supermarket', 'convenience', 'bakery')

After editing, run make db-apply to reload the function. Tag the PR with requires-schema-update. (When the tag filter changed too, requires-reimport already covers it.)

docs.title: Step 3 — Frontend: app/src/components/POIPanel.svelte → CATEGORIES
docs.text:
Each category in the CATEGORIES array has:

  • icon — emoji displayed next to the category
  • label — the translated category name, $_('poi.categories.<name>') (not the bare key)
  • match — function that tests a POI's tags (must match the SQL filter)
  • fallback — the translated text shown when no POIs are found, $_('poi.fallbacks.<name>')
  • hint (optional) — function returning an extra line per POI, e.g. a bus stop's direction

To add a new category, add an entry to the array. To add an OSM tag to an existing category, extend its match function.

docs.title: Step 4 — Translations (if adding a new category)
docs.text: Add poi.categories.<name> and poi.fallbacks.<name> keys to locales/en.json and locales/de.json in the same commit. The other locale files belong to Weblate; see Translation Workflow.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text: Run make db-apply (and make import if you changed the tag filter), then open a playground near a matching place and check that the panel lists it under the new category, and shows the fallback text where there is none.

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text: Branch, commit and open the pull request as described in Local Development → Start here. Tag it requires-reimport if you changed the tag filter, otherwise requires-schema-update.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Import Pipeline: how the osmium filter and api.sql fit together
  • API reference → get_pois

docs.title: Add a Sport Pitch Type
docs.text: Playground maps often include sports pitches — football fields, basketball courts, skate parks, BMX tracks, and many more. Each pitch type is identified by the OSM sport tag on a leisure=pitch feature. Adding a new sport type means adding translations to both locale files so the app shows a readable label instead of a tidied-up tag value (roller_hockey → "Roller hockey").

docs.title: Step 1 — Find the OSM tag value
docs.text:
OSM uses the tag sport=<value> on leisure=pitch features. The full list of documented values is at:

  • wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:sport
  • wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:leisure%3Dpitch

For example, a roller hockey rink uses sport=roller_hockey.

Finding pitches with a specific sport in OSM

Use Overpass Turbo — search for leisure=pitch + sport=roller_hockey (replace with your value) to confirm the tag is used in the wild.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add the translation keys
docs.text:
Open locales/en.json and add a new entry under equipment.pitches:

"pitches": {
  "soccer":        "Football pitch",
  "basketball":    "Basketball court",
  ...
  "roller_hockey": "Roller hockey rink"
}

The key must exactly match the OSM sport tag value (case-sensitive, underscores preserved).

Then open locales/de.json and add the German translation at the same path:

"pitches": {
  "soccer":        "Bolzplatz",
  "basketball":    "Basketballfeld",
  ...
  "roller_hockey": "Rollhockeyfeld"
}

Both files must be updated — a key missing from de.json shows the English text (fallbackLocale: 'en'); only a key missing from en.json too falls back to the tag value with underscores replaced and the first letter capitalised.

There is a second namespace for the sport on its own, pitch.sports.<value> ("Roller hockey" rather than "Roller hockey rink"). The panel of a pitch outside a playground (PitchPanel) shows its sports as chips from it, and the hover tooltip uses it when equipment.pitches has no entry. Add the key there too, in both files:

"pitch": {
  "sports": {
    ...
    "roller_hockey": "Roller hockey"
  }
}

Two optional extras, both code changes: a sport-specific pin symbol in BY_SPORT in app/src/lib/sportGlyphs.js (otherwise the generic flag), and an illustration in pitchImages in app/src/lib/equipmentAttributes.js, which then needs make equipment-images (Update Generated Assets).

docs.title: Step 3 — Handle multi-value sport tags (no extra work needed)
docs.text: OSM allows semicolon-separated multi-values on sport (e.g. sport=cycling;bmx). The equipment list automatically splits on ;, translates each part using the keys above, and joins them with /. Unknown values fall back to the raw OSM string. You only need to add the individual keys — no extra code changes are required.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
make dev

Open the app at http://localhost:5173, navigate to a playground that contains a pitch with your sport tag, and check the equipment list. The pitch should show your translated label. For a pitch outside any playground, turn on Sports pitches (outside playgrounds) in the filter panel and open it.

Finding a playground with a specific pitch

Use Overpass Turbo to locate an OSM node or way with leisure=pitch and sport=<your_value>, note its coordinates, and navigate there in the app.

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text: Branch, commit and open the pull request as described in Local Development → Start here. The change touches only locales/en.json and locales/de.json.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Equipment Types → Sport pitch images

docs.title: Frontend Contributor Guide
docs.text: This guide explains how the Svelte 5 frontend is structured, how data flows through it, and how to make common types of changes. It assumes you have local dev set up.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
main.js
  └── StandaloneApp.svelte  or  HubApp.svelte
        ├── Map.svelte             (OpenLayers map, all layers)
        ├── PlaygroundPanel.svelte (detail panel for selected playground)
        │     └── panel/*          (zones shared with PitchPanel, see below)
        ├── FilterPanel.svelte     (filter dropdown)
        ├── SearchBar.svelte       (Nominatim search)
        └── ...

The app mounts either StandaloneApp or HubApp based on appMode from lib/config.js. The two modes share most components; the hub adds federation components in src/hub/.

docs.title: State management
docs.text:
The app uses Svelte writable stores (src/stores/). Components import stores directly — there is no top-down prop drilling for shared state.

Store Shape Who writes Who reads selection { feature: OlFeature\|null, backendUrl: string, kind: 'playground'\|'pitch' }; derived hasSelection, selectedKind, selectedOsmId Map.svelte (click), AppShell (deeplink restore) PlaygroundPanel, PitchPanel, AppShell (panel slot) filterStore { private: bool, water: bool, baby: bool, … } FilterPanel, MappingDetailControl, FilterChips the popovers' own checkboxes — everything else reads effectiveFilterStore modalOpen boolean (derived from a counter) the modal action on each dialog element Map.svelte (Escape handler) effectiveFilterStore derived from filterStore + mappingDetail — Map.svelte (polygon visibility), StandaloneApp/HubApp (tier refetch → cluster params, macro aggregates), FilterChips mappingDetail boolean (default false; localStorage + ?detail=1\|0) MappingDetailControl Map.svelte (cluster/polygon/macro style), AppShell (legend), PlaygroundPanel (share link), effectiveFilterStore activeTierStore null \| 'cluster' \| 'polygon' \| 'macro' tieredOrchestrator Map.svelte (layer visibility) overlayFeaturesStore { equipment: [], trees: [] } PlaygroundPanel Map.svelte (equipment/tree layers) playgroundSourceStore OL VectorSource | null Map.svelte AppShell (deeplink hydration), ReportMissingFlow (duplicate check) mapStore OL Map | null Map.svelte LocateButton, other map-interacting components location { lat, lon, accuracy } \| null LocateButton (manual + auto-locate) Map.svelte (location marker), PlaygroundPanel (navigation origin) regionFramingApplied null \| true \| false (region-URL framing outcome; false → unresolved, map left at default extent) StandaloneApp LocateButton (auto-locate centering decision) hubLoadingStore { loaded, total, settling } hubOrchestrator nothing at the moment — the region pill's progress comes from the registry store macroFilteredStore Map<backendUrl, {count, complete, partial, missing}> \| null hubOrchestrator (macro tier, filter active) MacroView macroCoverageStore { answered, total, cantFilter[], settling } \| null hubOrchestrator (macro tier, filter active) MacroView, MacroCoverageBanner outsideBasemapCoverage null \| boolean (no limit declared / inside / outside BASEMAP_COVERAGE_BBOX) Map.svelte (moveend) BasemapCoverageNotice dataCoverage [{ url, bbox, slug?, name? }] \| null — where this map has data StandaloneApp, HubApp ReportMissingFlow (outside it: no duplicate check, MapComplete only) installPrompt the browser's beforeinstallprompt event | null the store module itself (listens for the event) DataContributionModal (Install as app) reportStep / reportPlacing null \| 'place' \| 'dupe' \| 'choose' \| 'form' \| 'done' / derived boolean startReport() from every entry point (AppShell button, SearchBar no-hits, About dialog, ReportMissingFlow's empty-area hint) ReportMissingFlow (the steps), AppShell (hides controls), Map.svelte (click does not select while placing)

docs.title: Selection flow
docs.text:
The selection is a playground or a standalone pitch (#934; in the hub too since #947): selection.select(feature, backendUrl, kind) with kind 'playground' (default) or 'pitch'. One store with a kind keeps "only one thing is open" true by construction. hasSelection means "anything is open" (it drives the shared panel slot and the mobile layout); selectedKind says which; selectedOsmId is the selected playground's id only. Anything that only makes sense for a playground — PlaygroundPanel's equipment, trees, POIs and reviews — must check the kind. A pitch is selected by a click on a layer the shell marks selectable (the pitch layer from lib/pitchLayer.js, not a selected playground's equipment overlay), writes #P<osm_id> (in the hub #<slug>/P<osm_id>; a slug-less hub link is resolved by asking every backend), and opens PitchPanel in the playground panel's slot; its display rules (every fact only when tagged) live in lib/pitchInfo.js.

User clicks playground polygon
        │
        ▼
Map.svelte click handler
  → selection.select(feature, backendUrl)
  → writes URL hash (#W<osm_id>)
        │
        ▼
PlaygroundPanel subscribes to selection
  → fetches equipment + trees + POIs + reviews
  → writes overlayFeaturesStore
        │
        ▼
Map.svelte subscribes to overlayFeaturesStore
  → updates equipment and tree OL layers

docs.title: Filter flow
docs.text:
User toggles filter in FilterPanel / MappingDetailControl
        │
        ▼
filterStore updated ──► effectiveFilterStore (completeness states forced on
        │                while mapping detail is off)
        │
        ├──► Map.svelte: polygon layer re-renders
        │    (matchesFilters() hides non-matching polygons)
        │
        └──► tieredOrchestrator.rerun()
             → re-fetches cluster tier with active filters as query params

Each zoom tier applies filters through a different path:

Tier Filter path polygon client-side — matchesFilters() hides non-matching polygons in Map.svelte cluster server-side — active filters become filter_* query params on get_playground_clusters macro (hub) derived — see below

docs.title: Macro tier (hub) filter path
docs.text:
The macro tier is normally zero-fetch: MacroView.svelte renders one ring per backend straight from the cached get_meta totals, and panning at min zoom dispatches no requests. get_meta has no filter dimension, so when a filter is active those totals would ignore it.

When a filter is active, hubOrchestrator instead fans out the filter-aware get_playground_clusters RPC once per backend (scoped to each backend's own bbox), sums the returned buckets into a per-backend {count, complete, partial, missing}, and publishes it progressively on macroFilteredStore. MacroView overrides each ring's props from that store as entries settle; a backend with no entry yet (or a pre-tier peer that 404s) keeps its cached-meta ring. Clearing all filters sets the store back to null and restores the zero-fetch path.

Alongside the filtered aggregate, hubOrchestrator publishes coverage on macroCoverageStore — { answered, total, cantFilter[], settling } where total is the in-scope healthy backends, answered is those that returned a filtered total, cantFilter lists backends that couldn't apply the filter (no bbox, or a 404 on the cluster RPC), and settling is true while the fan-out is still in flight. Those backends keep their unfiltered ring but are flagged _cantFilter so they render the distinct "unfiltered" variant instead of silently reading as a filtered subset, and MacroCoverageBanner shows "filter covers N of M regions" whenever answered < total once the fan-out has settled (settling === false) — so a normal load doesn't flash "covers 0 of N" mid-fetch, while an all-legacy hub still never silently presents partial coverage as complete (#688).

Macro ring variants (hub/macroRingStyle.js), in macroRingStyleFn priority order: offline (dashed grey) → importing (blue "updating") → cantFilter (full segments + dashed grey halo + "unfiltered" — backend couldn't apply the filter, so its whole catalogue is shown, marked as such) → filtered-empty (grey "no match" — healthy backend, but the filter excludes every playground) → degraded (amber "no data" — backend reachable but empty) → healthy (filled segments + count). Backend-health states outrank the filter outcome; "cant-filter" is a partial-coverage condition that outranks the filter results so it's never mistaken for a filtered ring; "no match" is distinct from the amber "no data" degraded ring.

docs.title: Runtime configuration
docs.text:
lib/config.js reads window.APP_CONFIG (written by oci/app/docker-entrypoint.sh at container startup) and exports named constants. In dev (no container), the constants use hardcoded defaults.

Config constants used across the codebase:

Constant Default Notes appMode 'standalone' 'standalone' or 'hub' apiBaseUrl '' Empty → Overpass fallback osmRelationId 62700 Fulda (dev default) clusterMaxZoom 13 Zoom threshold for tier switch macroMaxZoom 7 Hub macro view threshold defaultLocale '' UI language; empty → browser language → en regionLang 'de' Language the served OSM data is named in regionCountry 'de' Country for opening_hours holiday resolution regionState '' Optional state refinement; empty → library default openingHoursAddress derived { country_code, state? } for the opening_hours constructor — use this, never a literal

docs.title: The tiered orchestrator
docs.text:
lib/tieredOrchestrator.js is the data-fetching heart of standalone mode. attachTieredOrchestrator() wires to the OL map's moveend event and:

  1. Determines the active tier from view.getZoom() vs clusterMaxZoom
  2. Publishes the tier to activeTierStore
  3. Cancels any in-flight request via AbortController
  4. Calls the right API function (fetchPlaygroundClusters or fetchPlaygroundsBbox)
  5. Populates the corresponding OL VectorSource

The orchestrator is created in StandaloneApp.svelte on mount and torn down on destroy.

docs.title: Cluster buckets: grouping, position and merging
docs.text:
The standalone client switches between two zoom-scoped layers at clusterMaxZoom (default 13). Below the boundary it calls get_playground_clusters(z, bbox) for pre-aggregated count buckets; above it, get_playgrounds_bbox(bbox) for full polygons. The cluster RPC keeps two concerns deliberately separate: grouping is grid-based — each playground centroid is snapped to a zoom-dependent cell that decides which features share a bucket — while position is the unweighted spatial mean of the bucket's member centroids, so the rendered dot tracks the geography of its members rather than the lattice.

Because a grid cell is about as wide as a marker (≈ 64 px at z12 against a ≈ 52 px disc), neighbouring buckets routinely touch: two playgrounds 300 m apart on either side of a cell border become a disc and a pin side by side. Both modes therefore merge buckets client-side before drawing them (lib/clusterMerge.js, #941): buckets whose markers would overlap at the current resolution are combined, counts and completeness segments summed, the position the count-weighted mean. Marker size follows the count (radiusForCount), a single playground is sized as the finder pin in both modes, and passes repeat until nothing overlaps, since a merge grows the disc. In hub mode (see Federation reference) the same merge runs over all backends' buckets together, which is what removes the seam where two backends meet.

See API reference — get_playground_clusters for the response shape.

docs.title: OpenLayers layers
docs.text:
Map.svelte owns the basemap and most overlays; two more are added by the modules that own them:

Layer zIndex Owner Visible when macroOutlineLayer -1 Map.svelte Hub macro tier (world outline under the basemap) basemap 0 Map.svelte Always (vector tile or raster) pitchLayer 9 lib/pitchLayer.js filterStore.standalonePitches is on and zoom ≥ 12 playgroundLayer 10 Map.svelte $activeTierStore === 'polygon' clusterLayer 12 Map.svelte $activeTierStore === 'cluster' macroLayer 14 Map.svelte $activeTierStore === 'macro' (hub) treeLayer 15 Map.svelte A playground is selected equipmentLayer 20 Map.svelte A playground is selected own sent hints 25 ReportMissingFlow.svelte The visitor kept sent hints; zoom ≥ 11 locationLayer 30 Map.svelte A GPS position is known

Layer visibility is driven by reactive $: statements that subscribe to the stores above.

docs.title: Basemap layers
docs.text:
The basemap is configuration-driven (app/src/lib/config.js), not hardcoded:

  • basemapStyleUrl set → a VectorTileLayer styled with ol-mapbox-style, which is dynamically imported so raster deployments do not carry its ~310 kB.
  • otherwise → an XYZ TileLayer built from basemapUrl.

Two things are easy to get wrong here, and both were caught in review:

  • Attribution belongs to the source, not the layer. OpenLayers resolves it via layer.getSource().getAttributions(), so passing attributions as a layer option silently does nothing. On the vector path it must be applied after applyStyle() has created the source.
  • The vector fallback is gated on basemapUrlIsExplicit. When a style fails to load, falling back to basemapUrl is only safe if the operator set it; the compiled-in default is a third party that a vector deployment may have chosen vector to avoid.

macroOutlineLayer (zIndex -1) draws a bundled Natural Earth world outline under the hub macro tier, fetched lazily on first use from /basemap/world-110m.json (absolute — a relative path breaks under region URLs). It exists because the basemap tileset covers only the federation's own countries.

docs.title: Deeplinks
docs.text:
lib/deeplink.js handles URL hash encode/decode (parseHash, writeHash). The letter says what is selected — W a playground, P a standalone pitch:

  • #W<osm_id> / #P<osm_id> — standalone (no slug)
  • #<slug>/W<osm_id> / #<slug>/P<osm_id> — hub (slug identifies the backend; a slug-less pitch link is resolved by asking every backend)

selection.select() automatically writes the hash. On page load, AppShell.svelte reads the hash and dispatches fetchPlaygroundByOsmId to hydrate the polygon source before selecting.

docs.title: Adding a new filter
docs.text: Step by step, from the database flag to the filter chip: Add a Filter. The one rule to know when reading the filter code: anything that fetches or draws reads effectiveFilterStore, never filterStore (see Filter flow).

docs.title: The detail panels
docs.text:
PlaygroundPanel and PitchPanel are ordered by the parent's question (#1077), in three zones marked data-testid="zone-a|zone-b|zone-c":

Zone Playground Pitch A — decide header, mapper tools (mapping detail on), photos, pills (baby, toddler, shade, wheelchair, fenced, dogs), "what kids can do" (highlights, then activities) — or the contribution invitation header, sports, photos or example illustration, access / fee / booking B — go deeper description, "good to know" list, nearby (nearest per kind), all equipment (collapsed), reviews (collapsed) surface, lighting, hoops, opening hours, wheelchair C — background operator, contact, data age, MapComplete operator, MapComplete

Both are built from src/components/panel/:
