Component Role PanelHeader Title (with lang), place, hub region, access badge, navigate, share, close PhotoStrip Commons + Panoramax; a compact "no photo yet · add" line when empty; reports status (loading / photos / none) PillRow In this order: baby, toddler (for_baby / for_toddler), shade (lib/shade.js, reads the raw shade tag), wheelchair tri-state, fenced, dogs allowed ActivityRow The "what kids can do" block: HighlightsLine first, then the activities from lib/activities.js HighlightsLine Themes, water play, catalogue highlights MapperTools Mapping-detail badge, next-step hint, MapComplete — only while mapping detail is on ContributeInvite Replaces zone A when nothing is known, after equipment has loaded; its "tell us what is there" opens the hint (#1073). Otherwise PlaygroundPanel ends zone A with a "something missing? send a hint" link under the activities ZoneBackground Zone C; DataAgeChip holds the data-age popover

Rules:

  • Mapping detail adds, it never reorders. The tool block appears under the header; the MapComplete link moves between it and zone C.
  • Anything a visitor can filter by is visible in the panel when it applies. A new filter needs a place in a zone.
  • Activities and highlights come from the catalogue. Every device in objPlaygroundEquipment.js declares activity (one of ACTIVITIES in lib/activities.js, or null) and highlight; activities.test.js fails when one is missing. Both read separately mapped devices and the area-level playground:<device>=yes|<n> tags.

docs.title: Hints about a known playground (#1073)
docs.text:
The "missing playground" flow (ReportMissingFlow, stores/reportMissing.js) has a second entry: startHint(target) opens the dialog at its form step with reportTarget set (OSM type and id, interior point, known device keys, fence/shade/name known, MapComplete URL). Unlike startReport() it keeps the selection, so the dialog's history entry sits on top of the panel's and back returns to the panel. The panel's Escape handler stands down while a report step is open (ReportMissingFlow marks the event with preventDefault).

The form hides what is known, offers shade and a name only for a target, and buildNoteText({ target }) writes a note with the object link and area tags (playground:<device>=yes, shade=*). Chips come from REPORT_EQUIPMENT (14 devices, shared by both flows) with the icon of the device's activity (deviceIcon() in lib/activities.js). The session limit is shared. A hint cannot be sent empty, gets no own-note pin (it would sit on the playground's interior point and swallow taps meant for it), and its link under the activities appears only once equipment has loaded. selection.js ignores landing on a report entry, and reportMissing.js steps back off a stale one, so browser Forward after closing a hint does not close the panel.

docs.title: Internationalisation
docs.text:
New UI strings go into locales/en.json and locales/de.json in the same commit, and no other locale file is edited by hand. The full workflow, including how strings reach Weblate and back: Translation Workflow → Adding new UI strings.

Translations live in locales/*.json and are loaded by lib/i18n.js using svelte-i18n. In components, use the $_ store, as every component does:

<script>
  import { _ } from 'svelte-i18n';
</script>

<p>{$_('myKey')}</p>

Translation to other languages happens via Weblate.

docs.title: Example illustrations and failed images
docs.text: Device and pitch illustrations are HTML strings from lib/equipmentAttributes.js (illustrationHtml), rendered with {@html}. They carry no inline onerror: the narrowed CSP (script-src 'self', #861) blocks inline handlers. lib/imageFallback.js, installed once in main.js, listens for error in the capture phase and hides a failed image's .device-img-wrap — and an enclosing [data-illustration] section, so no empty heading is left. New {@html} images should use the same wrapper rather than an inline handler.

docs.title: Modal dialogs
docs.text: Every role="dialog" aria-modal="true" element carries use:modal from stores/modalOpen.js (#758). While it is mounted, everything outside the dialog — each sibling of the dialog and of its ancestors up to <body> — is inert, focus moves into the dialog, and on close it returns to where it was. aria-modal alone does none of that: before this, Tab walked from a dialog's last control onto the focusable map behind it (arrow keys then panned a map nobody could see), the search bar and the control buttons. Nested dialogs stack — a lightbox over another dialog makes that dialog inert and hands it back. modalOpen lets window-level handlers stand down while a dialog is up (Map's Escape for the hub popup). tests/modal-inert.spec.js pins it. The hub's instance drawer is a side panel, not an overlay, and traps Tab itself, so it does not register.

docs.title: Codes that must be read as words
docs.text: A short code shown as text — the hub drawer's country chip (SK, #741) — is read letter by letter ("ess kay"). aria-label cannot fix that on a plain <span>: ARIA forbids naming the generic role and screen readers ignore it there. Hide the code with aria-hidden="true" and put the full name next to it in a visually-hidden span (Bootstrap's class); a title can carry the same name for mouse users. Get names from Intl.DisplayNames in the active locale rather than locale keys, so Weblate translators have nothing to chase.

docs.title: Language attributes
docs.text:
Two languages coexist on the page, and mixing them up is a WCAG failure:

  • Interface text is in the UI locale. setupI18n() writes it to document.documentElement.lang, so translated strings need no lang of their own — they inherit the right one. (index.html still ships a static lang="de"; it is overwritten during init, before anything renders.)
  • OSM-derived text — playground names, and anything else read straight from a tag — is in the region's language, not the interface's. Every element rendering it carries lang={regionLang}.

The rule matters most where the two meet. getPlaygroundTitle() returns either OSM name tags or the translated nearby.defaultName placeholder, and the returned string cannot tell you which. Ask hasOsmName(attr):

$: titleLang = hasOsmName(attr) ? regionLang : $locale;
…
<h2 lang={titleLang}>{getPlaygroundTitle(attr, $_)}</h2>

Current name render sites: HoverPreview, panel/PanelHeader (used by PlaygroundPanel and PitchPanel, both of which pass titleLang). If you add another, annotate it — an unannotated name silently inherits the interface language.

docs.title: The search combobox
docs.text:
SearchBar.svelte implements the ARIA 1.2 combobox pattern over the Nominatim suggestion list. If you touch it, keep these invariants:

  • The input owns the list. role="combobox" + aria-autocomplete="list" + aria-controls pointing at the results container's id, aria-expanded mirroring list visibility, aria-busy mirroring the in-flight request. Ids come from a module-scoped counter (searchbar-<n>-…) — the component is in Svelte legacy mode, so $props.id() is unavailable.
  • DOM focus never leaves the input. Arrow keys move an activeIndex exposed via aria-activedescendant; options are not tab stops (tabindex="-1"). Roving tabindex would break continued typing. The tab order is input → clear button → out of the card.
  • Options stay real <button>s. Touch screen readers (TalkBack, VoiceOver) navigate with a virtual cursor that ignores aria-activedescendant and activates elements in place, so options must be natively activatable. role="option" overrides the button role without conflict.
  • Dismissal is focus containment, never a timer. focusout on .search-card tests currentTarget.contains(e.relatedTarget). The old 200 ms hide timer raced both a mouse click in Safari and a touch scroll inside the list on iOS.
  • mousedown, not pointerdown, is prevented on the results container. mousedown is synthesised after a tap completes, so suppressing it cannot break scrolling; pointerdown fires at touch start and would.
  • One highlight only. mousemove writes activeIndex and only .active is styled — a separate :hover rule would let the pointer highlight a different row than the one aria-activedescendant announces. activeIndex resets on every reassignment of results (search, clear, error path), since the 450 ms debounce can swap the result set under a stale index.

Regression coverage: tests/searchbar-a11y.spec.js (stubs Nominatim via page.route). Safari mouse selection, iOS scroll-in-list, and TalkBack navigation are manual-only — Playwright's Chromium does not reproduce those quirks.

docs.title: Playground themes
docs.text:
playground:theme=* (OSM) is meant to describe a whole playground's motto — a ship, castle, or octopus playground. The tag reaches the frontend on both the playground polygon and equipment features via the hstore_to_jsonb(tags) merge in api.sql (it is not an osm2pgsql column, so it is not stripped).

In practice the key is dominated by two kinds of non-theme usage: tagging noise (playground/play are ~53% of all uses) and device-shape values — horse, duck, elephant, … tagged on a single playground=springy rider to describe its shape, not a playground theme. A springy can be shaped as anything, so those values are noise for our purposes. We therefore honour only an allowlist of documented whole-playground themes (SUPPORTED_THEMES in lib/playgroundThemes.js: ship, castle, spiderweb, water, adventure, rocket, dragon, octopus, circus). Everything else is dropped at the single splitThemes choke point, so it never reaches any consumer. Extend the allowlist by adding an entry to THEME_ICONS (the icon map is the allowlist) plus an equipAttr.themes.* label in each locale.

lib/playgroundThemes.js owns the presentation:

  • themeIcon(value) — curated emoji per allowlisted theme value. FALLBACK_ICON (✨) is a defensive backstop only; it never renders for non-allowlisted values, which are filtered out upstream.
  • themeName(value, t) — localised label from equipAttr.themes.*, falling back to the raw value.
  • themeOf(props) — the first allowlisted theme on a single feature, used for the inline device symbol.
  • areaThemesOf(props) — allowlisted themes on the playground's own area tag; that theme is worded "a … playground" in the highlights line.
  • aggregatePlaygroundThemes(areaProps, deviceProps) — deduped, ordered theme list for a playground (area theme first, then device themes by frequency). PlaygroundPanel passes it to highlightsOf(), so themes lead the highlights line in zone A; EquipmentList/EquipmentTooltip render the per-device symbol inline.

Themes are panel-only; showing them on the map is not planned yet.

docs.title: External services: implementation notes
docs.text: Which services the visitor's browser reaches, and why, is in External Services and Privacy by design. These are the implementation details behind it.

docs.title: Equipment illustrations are resolved at build time
docs.text:
The device and pitch tables name their illustrations as MediaWiki File: titles. Turning one into a URL used to mean a Special:FilePath request, which is a redirect chain, and that chain cannot be proxied without allowing /w/index.php — a full MediaWiki entry point — through the cache.

So the redirect is followed at build time instead. tools/build-equipment-images.py resolves each name against Commons and then the OSM wiki, and commits app/src/lib/equipmentImages.generated.json holding the real file URL plus author and licence. Rebuild it with make equipment-images.

Three things follow from that, and each fixed a real defect:

  • The bytes come from this instance. The resolved URL is an ordinary image path on a MediaWiki file host, which /ext/wikimedia/<host>/ already serves.
  • The OSM wiki is no longer an undisclosed host. 14 of the 98 illustrations exist only there, and the frontend used to reach them through an <img onerror> fallback that appeared in neither this page nor the CSP. It is listed in External Services now, and it is proxied like the rest.
  • A name that resolves nowhere fails the build. 14 of them did, all pitch illustrations, and in production each one cost two failing requests before an onerror handler hid the element. They were replaced with verified Commons files in #867 (hockey, which has no free pitch diagram, has no illustration), so every name now resolves and any new one that does not fails the build.

docs.title: Checking what a panel section contacts
docs.text: PlaygroundPanel.svelte mounts each accordion section's component only while the section is open (openSections, empty by default: all equipment and reviews start collapsed), so a closed section's fetch code never runs. Reading a fetch call alone gives the wrong answer about when a service is contacted: check the section's default state too. Reviews start closed (tests/reviews-deferral.spec.js). One exception since #1077: while Mangrove is proxied (mangroveApiUrl same-origin, headerRatingEnabled in lib/reviews.js), the panel reads the reviews on selection to show the average under the name. The read goes through the same session cache, so opening the section later does not ask again; with the proxy off nothing changes. Photos are not an accordion section since #1077: panel/PhotoStrip loads Commons thumbnails on selection, as the open photos section did before, and Panoramax stays click-to-load.

docs.title: Reviews ask once per label
docs.text: Mangrove matches a review on its coordinates and its q label, and clients file playgrounds under different labels (spieli used osm_playground_<id>; MapComplete and mangrove.reviews use playground or the place's name). The reviews section asks once per label and merges the answers by signature (#914); new reviews are written under the shared label. The submit path is a PUT whose signature covers the JWT's own claims, so the proxy is transparent to verification.

docs.title: Keep the privacy template in sync
docs.text: oci/app/datenschutz.template.html carries a service table of its own. When a service is added or removed, update it together with External Services. Describe what the code does rather than claiming spieli "does not track users": that depends on each deployment's configuration.

docs.title: Settled questions — recorded so they are not re-investigated
docs.text:
• Commons URLs from OSM tags are host-validated in app/src/lib/commons.js before rendering, so a crafted image tag cannot point the browser at an arbitrary host. The Content Security Policy is a second line behind that check, not a replacement for it. Both are tested: tests/hostile-image-tag.spec.js and the CSP must follow the configuration CI job.
  • Which Wikimedia host serves a file is not fixed. The imageinfo API currently returns thumbnails on thumb.wikimedia.org and originals on upload.wikimedia.org. proxiedImageUrl therefore carries the original host in the proxy path rather than assuming one; a rewrite pinned to a single host silently sends every thumbnail straight to Wikimedia while appearing to work.

docs.title: Style system
docs.text: The app uses Bootstrap 5 (component classes) and Tailwind CSS 4 (utility classes) side by side. The design system primitives in src/components/ui/ (Badge, Button, Card, etc.) wrap Bootstrap with Tailwind utilities. Prefer these over raw Bootstrap classes in new components.

docs.title: The finder view (mapping detail off)
docs.text:
Mapping detail is opt-in (#924). With it off, Map.svelte swaps the tier styles for the ones in src/lib/finderStyle.js (cluster discs, pins at each playground's interior point, the selected playground's outline) and hub/macroRingStyle.js's finderMacroRingStyleFn (neutral discs; health variants unchanged). The FINDER colours sit in completenessPalette.js with their contrast measurements. Style functions take the mode from their caller rather than reading the store, so they stay pure and unit-testable. Canvas markers draw in CSS pixels through hidpiStyleOptions (lib/hidpiRenderer.js), which also supplies their 1:1 hit-detection renderer, so the existing click/hover path selects pins — but a click inside the undrawn polygon off the pin does not.

Whether mapping detail is on lives in stores/mappingDetail.js (persisted in localStorage, overridable per page load with ?detail=1|0). While it is off, the showComplete / showPartial / showMissing filters are ignored everywhere — rendering, cluster request parameters, badges, hub macro aggregates — via effectiveFilterStore; their stored values return when it is switched back on.

docs.title: The hint under the badge
docs.text: PlaygroundPanel passes the hint to panel/MapperTools (the tool block under the header) from mappingDetailHintKey() in completeness.js, which reads the same mappingDetailInputs() as playgroundCompleteness(), so hint and badge cannot disagree. The texts are mappingDetail.nextStep.*.

docs.title: Mapping-detail locale keys
docs.text:
All UI strings live under the mappingDetail.* namespace in locales/de.json and locales/en.json (repo root).

Key DE EN mappingDetail.legendTitle Erfasste Details Mapping detail mappingDetail.detailed detailliert detailed mappingDetail.basic grundlegend basic mappingDetail.noDetails keine Details no details yet mappingDetail.hasPhoto hat ein Foto has a photo

Access is a separate axis from mapping detail and has its own access.* namespace (#1002): access.private / access.customers for the panel badge and access.privateShort / access.customersShort for the hover chip. The rule behind them is accessKind() in app/src/lib/access.js.

The filter labels under filter.mappingDetail.* use the same wording (in German detailliert / grundlegend / keine Details); the filter keys themselves (showComplete, showPartial, showMissing) keep the identifier naming.

The label key mappingDetail.legendTitle ("Erfasste Details" / "Mapping detail") can be used wherever the concept needs a heading.

docs.title: Accent colour
docs.text:
The UI accent is one emerald family, defined once as theme tokens in src/styles/app.css (#930):

Token Value Use --color-primary #047857 buttons with text, links, accent text, active control icons, badges (Tailwind: bg-primary, text-primary) --color-primary-hover #065f46 hover / pressed --color-primary-soft #ecfdf5 background of an active control or checked row

Reference them with var(--color-primary) and friends, never as literals. The lighter emerald-500 (#10b981) the app used before is only 2.54:1 behind white text — every accent pair here clears 4.5:1. Map markers are the exception: canvas renderers cannot read CSS variables, so their colours live in completenessPalette.js.

docs.title: The mapping-detail palette
docs.text:
src/lib/completenessPalette.js is the single source of truth for the three mapping-detail colours (complete / partial / missing). Never hardcode these values anywhere else.

Each bucket exposes base, fill, stroke and hatch. The module documents which surface uses which field; the short version is that anything opaque takes base, and only shapes the basemap shows through — or backgrounds carrying text — take fill. Getting this wrong is silent: nothing errors, two surfaces simply render the same bucket in different colours.

Consumers today: vectorStyles.js (polygons), clusterStyle.js, hub/macroRingStyle.js, CompletenessLegend.svelte, PlaygroundPanel.svelte, MappingDetailControl.svelte, hub/InstancePanelDrawer.svelte.

Svelte <style> blocks cannot import, so components that colour elements via CSS classes read the palette in <script> and expose it as custom properties (--detail-complete and friends) on the wrapping element. InstancePanelDrawer follows that pattern — copy it rather than reintroducing literals.

docs.title: Why the arcs are cased
docs.text:
base is drawn opaque for cluster and macro ring arcs, and bright green cannot carry contrast on its own against this basemap: #4ade80 measures 1.59:1 on the background, 1.35:1 over grass and 1.06:1 over water, against a 3:1 floor for a graphical object. No green above 3:1 exists lighter than L* 31.

Moving the whole ramp down a step was tried first and cost more than it bought — the bright end disappeared, the ramp stopped being monotonic, and on the polygon tier partial and missing collapsed to ΔE 9.7, making the two lower buckets hard to separate.

Instead each arc is drawn over a dark casing one pixel proud on each side (RING_CASING), so the edge carries the contrast and the fill is free to be chosen for meaning. That is how road casings work in cartography. With the ramp restored, the same polygon pair is ΔE 20.2.

Known cost: the rings read heavier. missing is the dominant bucket — 625 of 926 playgrounds in Fulda — and slate-600 against a dark casing makes a mostly-unmapped cluster read as a near-black disc at low zoom. Kept for now. The levers are a lighter or thinner casing, or lightening missing, which the casing makes possible again. Note the tension there: monotonic lightness wants missing darkest, while "the least-mapped state should stay quiet" wants it lightest. This palette currently chooses the ordering.

Two rendering traps worth knowing:

  • OpenLayers' renderPolygonGeometry handles fill, stroke and text only. An image style attached to a Polygon is silently dropped — no render, no warning. Give it a geometry function returning the polygon's interior point.
  • hub/macroRingStyle.js colours restricted (violet-600) on a different axis from the mapping-detail buckets — access, not detail. deriveMacroRing sets restricted: 0 whenever a backend reports completeness and routes the whole count into it only when completeness is unknown, so restricted and missing never share a ring. They do sit side by side as separate rings on the same macro view, which is why the two colours still have to stay apart.

docs.text:

  • Testing Guide — how to write and run tests
  • Add a Playground Device — adding a new playground device type
  • Source Tree — annotated directory map

docs.title: Update Generated Assets
docs.text: Some files in the repository are generated by a make target and committed, so a build never depends on someone else's service being up. After changing their source, regenerate them and commit the result with your change.

docs.title: App icons
docs.text:
The installable-app icons live in app/public/icons/ (#939). icon-192.png and icon-512.png are the free-standing pin; the maskable variants that Android launchers and some desktops cut into a circle are generated from icon-512.png:

make app-icons            # rewrites app/public/icons/icon-maskable-{192,512}.png

Commit the regenerated files. They are served under stable names with a one-day cache, so an installed app picks up a new icon within a day.

docs.title: Holiday states
docs.text:
REGION_STATE is resolved against the state codes and names the opening_hours library knows, extracted into app/src/lib/holidayStates.generated.json. After bumping opening_hours, re-extract it:

make holiday-states       # rewrites app/src/lib/holidayStates.generated.json

A unit test fails while the table's recorded library version differs from the installed one, so a forgotten re-run does not go unnoticed.

docs.title: Equipment illustrations
docs.text:
The device and pitch tables (app/src/lib/objPlaygroundEquipment.js, app/src/lib/equipmentAttributes.js) name illustrations as MediaWiki File: titles. Those names are resolved to real file URLs at build time, so after adding or changing one:

make equipment-images     # re-resolve, rewriting app/src/lib/equipmentImages.generated.json

Commit the regenerated file with your change. It is checked in on purpose, like the basemap assets, so a build never depends on someone else's API being up.

Two things to expect:

  • A name that resolves on neither Commons nor the OSM wiki fails the target. That is the point: such a name used to render nothing while costing two failing requests. Fix the name, or drop the entry — there is no allow-list for missing files any more (#867).
  • The resolved URL is not Special:FilePath. It is the real file path on a Wikimedia or OSM-wiki host, which the /ext/wikimedia/ proxy serves, so the visitor's browser never contacts either wiki. Do not reintroduce a Special:FilePath URL in the frontend — CI rejects it.

make check-equipment-images re-resolves and fails if the committed map no longer points at the same files. It is not wired into CI, because it depends on two live APIs; run it by hand if illustrations start disappearing.

docs.title: Basemap style
docs.text:
make basemap-style produces two variants from a single upstream fetch, both vendored copies of OpenFreeMap Bright with the same two edits:

File Assets point at Used by app/public/basemap/style.json tiles.openfreemap.org make dev, which has no nginx to proxy through app/public/basemap/style.local.json /basemap/ on this instance the container — this is what visitors get

One fetch, both outputs: building them in two runs let the upstream rotate in between, leaving the two variants derived from different sources with nothing detecting it.

The two edits, applied by tools/build-basemap-style.py:

  1. Green landcover fills are desaturated, because spieli draws its playgrounds in green — emerald pins in the default view, a green-to-slate ramp with mapping detail on. A basemap that paints parks green competes with the map's primary signal.
  2. The poi symbol layers are dropped, as the strongest competitor for attention.

The second edit is a legibility change only. Dropping a style layer does not reduce render cost — the tile data is still decoded and simply not drawn.

--asset-base is what rewrites the style's tile, glyph and sprite URLs onto one origin, and it is the whole difference between a local style and a local basemap. Without it — which is how style.json is built — those assets are fetched from tiles.openfreemap.org by every visitor, even though the style document itself is served locally.

Only the origin is stripped; the upstream's own paths are preserved verbatim. That 1:1 mapping is what lets a plain prefix proxy serve the result without reversing a mapping it cannot know. The build refuses to write an --asset-base output that still contains a third-party host, and drops any query string it finds, so rebuilding against a keyed provider cannot bake an API key into a committed style.

make basemap-assets runs this together with make basemap-fonts and the world outline for the hub's macro view. How operators configure the basemap: Basemap and external services.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Add a Playground Device: where illustration names come from
  • Local Development

docs.title: How the hub works internally
docs.text:
What happens in the browser between a pan or zoom on the hub map and the rings, clusters and polygons it draws. The contract each backend has to meet (endpoints, ring states) is in the Federation reference; why spieli is federated at all, in Federation: one map, many owners.

The Hub is designed to stay responsive with anything from two to thirty backends without any per-deployment tuning. It does this with three zoom tiers and a bbox router, so a Europe-wide viewport doesn't pull every polygon from every backend, and a city-block viewport doesn't ship a redundant continental aggregate.

docs.title: Zoom tiers
docs.text:
Zoom Tier What ships per backend Where the work happens 0–7 (≤ macroMaxZoom) macro nothing — uses cached get_meta; with a filter active, get_playground_clusters(macroMaxZoom, backend bbox) per backend, summed into macroFiltered client renders one ring per backend at the bbox centroid 8–13 (≤ clusterMaxZoom) cluster get_playground_clusters(z, bbox) returns pre-aggregated buckets server bucketing + client re-clustering across border seams 14+ polygon get_playgrounds_bbox(bbox) returns full GeoJSON polygons client just concatenates per-backend polygons (each tagged with _backendUrl)

macroMaxZoom and clusterMaxZoom are independent config knobs (defaults 7 and 13). The macro tier is hub-only — standalone neither reads macroMaxZoom (the entrypoint writes it only into the hub's config.js) nor enters the macro tier.

docs.title: Bbox routing — only intersecting backends are queried
docs.text:
Every backend's get_meta response carries a bbox. On every (debounced) moveend, the Hub intersects the current viewport with each backend's bbox and only fans out to backends whose bbox intersects. A viewport over Berlin doesn't issue a request to a Köln-only backend; a viewport spanning the German-Polish border issues parallel requests to both backends.

The bboxes are refreshed on the registry poll (HUB_POLL_INTERVAL, default 5 minutes), so a backend that extends its OSM relation mid-session sees the change at the next poll without a hub restart.

docs.title: Fan-out and progressive render
docs.text:
The Hub invokes each selected backend's tier RPC in parallel via a single AbortController. As each backend's response arrives, the matching layer (cluster or polygon source) is repainted incrementally — a fast backend's contribution shows within ~100 ms even if a slower peer takes 2 seconds. Per-backend timeout is 5 s; a backend that exceeds it is omitted from the current tier with a one-time console warning, and the map stays interactive.

Every moveend constructs a fresh AbortController and aborts the previous one, so superseded fan-outs cancel their in-flight per-backend requests via the inner controller.

docs.title: Cross-backend re-clustering
docs.text:
At the cluster tier, two backends covering adjacent regions both ship their own bucket grids. Without re-clustering, the seam at their shared border shows as two overlapping rings. The Hub collects every backend's buckets and runs them through the same merge the standalone client uses (Frontend Guide → Cluster buckets), so two backends meet in a single seamless ring.

The polygon tier doesn't re-cluster — every backend's polygons render in a single vector source, each feature tagged with _backendUrl so selection routes back to the right backend.

At the macro tier the hub draws one ring per backend from cached get_meta data; which ring variant a backend gets is listed under Ring states.

docs.title: Architecture flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    user[User pans / zooms map] --> moveend[Debounced moveend<br/>300 ms]
    moveend --> tier{tierForZoom}
    tier -- "z ≤ 7" --> macro[Macro view<br/>cached get_meta;<br/>with a filter: clusters per backend]
    tier -- "z 8–13" --> cluster[Cluster tier]
    tier -- "z ≥ 14" --> polygon[Polygon tier]

    cluster --> bbox[bboxRouter.selectBackends<br/>viewport ∩ each bbox]
    polygon --> bbox

    bbox --> health[federationHealth.filterHealthy<br/>skip ok=false backends]
    health --> fanout[fanOut<br/>parallel AbortController<br/>per-backend 5 s timeout]

    fanout -- "cluster tier" --> sc[clusterMerge<br/>merge overlapping buckets, sum counts]
    fanout -- "polygon tier" --> concat[Concatenate features<br/>stamp _backendUrl]

    sc --> render[Repaint clusterSource<br/>incrementally per arrival]
    concat --> render2[Append to polygonSource<br/>incrementally per arrival]

    macro --> macroLayer[Render macroSource<br/>one ring per backend<br/>healthy/offline/importing/degraded]

Each box in the cluster/polygon path runs once per moveend. Fan-out is the only step that produces network traffic; everything else is in-memory.

docs.title: Import Pipeline
docs.text: This guide explains how OSM data flows from a Geofabrik PBF extract into the PostgreSQL database. It is aimed at contributors who want to add new OSM data types or change how existing data is processed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Geofabrik PBF (~300 MB state extract)
        │
        ▼  osmium extract (bbox clip — Nominatim lookup or OSM_BBOX override)
Bbox-clipped PBF (~5–20 MB)
        │
        ▼  osmium tags-filter
Tag-filtered PBF (~1–5 MB)
        │
        ▼  osm2pgsql --slim --drop --hstore
        │  (default pgsql output — no Lua script)
        │
        ▼  PostgreSQL tables (EPSG:3857)
        │   planet_osm_point    — OSM nodes
        │   planet_osm_line     — open ways (fences, boundary segments)
        │   planet_osm_polygon  — closed ways and relations as polygons
        │
        ▼  api.sql applied by import.sh
        │   ALTER SYSTEM (pg tuning)
        │   CREATE INDEX on planet_osm_* (idempotent)
        │   BUILD playground_stats under a staging name, then swap it in
        │   CREATE/REPLACE api schema functions
        │
        ▼  PostgREST /api/rpc/* endpoints

The pipeline is driven by importer/import.sh, which is the CMD of the importer Docker image (importer/Dockerfile).

docs.title: osm2pgsql and the hstore schema
docs.text:
osm2pgsql runs in its default pgsql output mode — no Lua flex script is involved. It imports the filtered PBF into standard tables (planet_osm_point, planet_osm_line, planet_osm_polygon), all in EPSG:3857. planet_osm_line matters for fences mapped as their own way (#773) and for region boundaries that do not close into a polygon.

A fixed set of common OSM keys get their own columns (name, operator, access, surface, leisure, amenity, sport, natural, highway, …). Every other tag is stored as a key→value pair in the tags hstore column. The --hstore flag enables this.

All application logic (computing completeness, deriving filter flags, building cluster counts) lives in importer/api.sql, which queries these standard tables.

docs.title: Adding a new attribute to an existing object type
docs.text:
Two distinct cases:

The object type is already imported (e.g. adding a new attribute to playground equipment nodes, which are already in the filter as n/playground):

  1. The tag value is already in the tags hstore — access it with tags->'my_tag' in importer/api.sql.
  2. Run make db-apply to apply the SQL change (no re-import needed).

The tag is used on a new object type not yet in the filter (e.g. amenity=drinking_water):

  1. Add the tag to the osmium tags-filter list in importer/import.sh. Otherwise the importer silently discards those objects.
  2. In importer/api.sql, add or extend a function to read the new data. Use tags->'my_tag' for hstore values or the named column for common keys.
  3. Run make import — the tag filter change requires a full re-import.

docs.title: Adding a new OSM object type
docs.text:
1. Add its tag to the osmium tags-filter list in importer/import.sh.
  2. In importer/api.sql, add a new PostgREST function that queries planet_osm_point or planet_osm_polygon (depending on geometry type). Follow the pattern of existing functions.
  3. Expose it: GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION api.your_function(...) TO web_anon;
  4. Run make import to load the data. Use make db-apply for subsequent SQL-only iterations.

Testing: there are no SQL unit tests. Verify changes with a real import (make import) against a region that has the relevant data, then check the feature appears correctly in the UI.

docs.title: The tag filter (importer/import.sh)
docs.text:
Before osm2pgsql runs, osmium tags-filter keeps only objects with tags the app actually queries. This is a performance optimisation — a state PBF goes from ~300 MB to ~1–5 MB. The current filter passes:

  • leisure=playground, leisure=pitch, leisure=fitness_station, leisure=picnic_table
  • amenity=bench, amenity=shelter, amenity=toilets, amenity=ice_cream, amenity=cafe, amenity=restaurant
  • natural=tree, natural=tree_row, playground=*
  • highway=bus_stop, shop=bakery/chemist/supermarket/convenience, emergency=*
  • barrier=fence ways — fences drawn around a playground (#773)
  • boundary=administrative, type=multipolygon

If you add a new OSM object type, add its tag to this filter — otherwise the importer will silently discard those objects.

The list lives in TAG_FILTERS, and the tag-filtered extract is cached next to a hash of it (*_tags.pbf.filter). Changing the list invalidates the cache on the next import, so the new tags arrive even when the source PBF has not changed. It still needs a full import — API_ONLY never runs osmium.

docs.title: The playground_stats materialised view
docs.text:
The most important post-import step in importer/api.sql is building the playground_stats materialised view. It pre-computes per-playground statistics (tree count, bench count, sport types, completeness state) so get_playgrounds_bbox is a fast indexed lookup rather than an aggregation query.

It is built entirely from the standard osm2pgsql tables:

  • Playground polygons and nodes come from planet_osm_polygon (leisure = 'playground') and planet_osm_point.
  • Equipment and trees are joined from planet_osm_point and planet_osm_polygon using spatial containment (ST_Intersects / ST_DWithin). Trees count within 15 m of the playground. A distance in metres must go through public.metres_to_3857(metres, lat) before it is compared to way: EPSG:3857 units shrink by cos(latitude), so a bare 15 covers only ~9.5 m in Hessen.
  • Less common tags (e.g. panoramax, opening_hours) are read from the tags hstore column.

docs.title: How the rebuild avoids an outage
docs.text:
The view is not dropped and recreated in place. api.sql builds it under the staging name playground_stats_new, indexes it, and then swaps it in inside a single DO block:

DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW IF EXISTS public.playground_stats CASCADE;
ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW public.playground_stats_new RENAME TO playground_stats;

The build is the long statement — minutes on a state-sized region. Dropping first meant the view was absent for that whole window, and every reader of it (get_meta, both map tiers) failed with relation "public.playground_stats" does not exist. Since the daemon importer re-applies api.sql on every container start, that made any routine restart a multi-minute API outage (#720). With the swap, readers keep the old view until the rename commits.

A DO block rather than a literal BEGIN/COMMIT because both callers must stay atomic: import.sh runs the file with plain psql -f (autocommit), make db-apply runs it with --single-transaction.

The planet_osm_* indexes are created before the build for the same reason — the build joins against those tables, so it is the statement that needs them.

The PostgREST connections are terminated inside the same transaction as the swap, not in a statement ahead of it. PostgREST reconnects on its own, so terminating separately leaves a gap in which a fresh connection can take a read lock — and the swap's pending AccessExclusiveLock then queues ahead of every later reader, stalling API traffic for as long as that straggler runs. In one transaction there is no gap.

Disk headroom: the staging view coexists with the live one, so peak disk use for playground_stats and its indexes is roughly double the steady-state size during a rebuild. Negligible for a city-sized region (Fulda's view is ~230 kB) but worth checking before an apply on a state-sized node with a nearly full volume.

The completeness logic in api.sql must stay in sync with app/src/lib/completeness.js in the frontend. Both implement the same rule:

Criterion SQL (api.sql) JS (completeness.js) Has equipment a playground=* object inside the area, or a soccer / basketball / table-tennis pitch device_count > 0 \|\| table_tennis_count > 0 \|\| has_soccer \|\| has_basketball Has info surface set, or access set and not 'yes', or opening_hours set !!(props.opening_hours \|\| props.surface \|\| (props.access && props.access !== 'yes'))
  • complete = both criteria present
  • partial = exactly one present
  • missing = neither

docs.title: Mapping detail rule
docs.text:
The rule itself, and why it is what it is, is explained in Mapping detail.

The identifiers complete / partial / missing are wire and storage values — they appear in API responses, in playground_stats, and in the filterStore keys. They deliberately differ from the labels shown to users (detailed / basic / no details yet); renaming them would break federation between backends on different versions.

The rule is maintained in two mirrored places that must stay in sync:

  • Frontend: app/src/lib/completeness.js — playgroundCompleteness(props) and hasPhotoSignal(props)
  • Database: importer/api.sql, CTE completeness_attrs feeding the playground_stats materialised view

Both sides are guarded. Case 17 in app/src/lib/completeness.test.js walks the truth table in JS. The "Assert JS/SQL rule parity" step in .github/workflows/db-smoke.yml does the SQL side by reading the live view definition rather than restating it: it extracts the has_equipment expression and fails if it stops counting any of device_count / table_tennis_count / has_soccer / has_basketball, or if it starts counting street furniture or a derived flag again (#776). It then checks the classification CASE still reads has_equipment AND has_info and has not taken has_photo back as an input. app/src/lib/completeness.js is one of the workflow's path triggers, so a change to the JS half alone still runs it.

Run make db-apply after changing the SQL definition to rebuild the materialised view. No re-import is needed — the view is derived.

docs.title: Persisted criterion columns
docs.text:
playground_stats stores the criteria alongside the derived state, as non-null booleans:

Column Criterion has_photo photo signal (not a state input; drives the marker) has_equipment hasEquipment above has_info hasInfo above

They are not exposed through any API function — they exist so the composition of each state can be measured directly instead of re-derived:

SELECT completeness, has_equipment, has_info, has_photo, count(*)
FROM playground_stats
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4
ORDER BY 5 DESC;

This is the query to run before and after any change to the criteria, to see which criterion is actually gating a state.

Street furniture does not count as equipment. Benches, shelters and picnic tables are often mapped inside a playground area by someone who never mapped the play equipment, so counting them lifts playgrounds that have nothing to play on. The flags derived from equipment tags (is_water, for_baby, for_toddler, for_wheelchair) are excluded for the same reason — a bench carrying wheelchair=yes is the same false signal through a side door (#776).

A photo is not a criterion. Photo tags are rare in OSM, so requiring one for the top bucket gated whole regions out of it. Availability is still derived — has_photo on playground_stats, hasPhotoSignal() in JS — but only to drive an additive marker, never the state. name and operator are not criteria either: administrative data, not useful to a parent choosing a playground.

Full rationale in Mapping detail.

If you change the completeness criteria, update both files and rebuild the materialised view with make db-apply.

docs.title: Filter flags (for_baby, for_toddler, is_water, …)
docs.text:
Several boolean columns in playground_stats are computed from equipment found inside each playground polygon (for_baby, for_toddler, is_water, wheelchair_play / for_wheelchair, has_soccer, has_basketball, has_fence, has_dogs, has_theme, has_shade, has_lit). They drive both the filter UI and the filter_attrs payload in the cluster RPC. Which tags set each one: OSM Tags spieli Reads → Filters.

Two of them mirror a frontend rule. has_lit (public.lit_state() ↔ litState() in app/src/lib/pitchInfo.js) is guarded in CI: both run over the truth table app/src/lib/litState.cases.json. The theme allowlist (↔ SUPPORTED_THEMES in app/src/lib/playgroundThemes.js) is kept in sync by hand.

All flag logic lives in importer/api.sql (the equip_stats CTE inside playground_stats).

Adding a flag and the filter that uses it: Add a Filter.

docs.title: Applying schema changes without a full re-import
docs.text:
make db-apply runs only the api.sql step (skips the osm2pgsql data load). Use it when: - You added or changed a PostgREST function - You changed the playground_stats view definition - You added a new filter flag

Do a full make import when you changed the tag filter (new object types needed in the PBF) — these affect which objects are stored in planet_osm_* tables.

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text: Requirements: Node.js 20.19 or newer (Vite 8 needs it; CI runs Node 20), Docker with the Compose plugin

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Set up the stack below, and run the tests once (Testing Guide).
  2. Get the picture: Architecture, then Tech Stack.
  3. Read the guide for the part you will touch: Frontend Guide, Import Pipeline, or How the hub works internally.
  4. For a typical first change, follow a how-to: Add a Playground Device, Add a Sport Pitch Type, Add a POI Category, Add a Filter.

How changes get in: open an issue first, branch from main as <type>/<issue>-<short-description>, write Conventional Commits, and open a pull request against mfuhrmann/spieli. New UI strings go into locales/en.json and locales/de.json only; the other locale files belong to Weblate (Translation Workflow). The full walkthrough: CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env
make install      # install Node dependencies (once)
make up           # start db + PostgREST + nginx; on first launch it also imports
                  # Fulda Stadt (454863) from the Hessen PBF — ~300 MB download
make dev          # Vite dev server with hot-reload at http://localhost:5173

make up runs make import by itself when the database has no api schema yet. Run make import again later to refresh the data.

For quick testing without the download, load the bundled fixture (4 Fulda playgrounds) before the first make up. It contains the api schema, so make up then skips the import:

make seed-load
make up

Run make help to list all available targets.

compose.yml is this development stack, not the compose.prod.yml the installer sets up for operators: it always starts the database, the API and the app, plus a second database and API (db2, postgrest2) for hub testing, whatever DEPLOY_MODE says. To work on a different region, set OSM_RELATION_ID and PBF_URL in .env (how to find them) and run make import. SQL-only changes to importer/api.sql are applied with make db-apply, without a re-import.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
Path Role app/src/ Svelte 5 frontend components and modules importer/ Import script (import.sh: osmium filter + osm2pgsql) and PostgREST API SQL (api.sql) db/ PostgreSQL schema initialisation oci/ Docker build contexts

For a file-by-file tour, see Source Tree.

docs.title: Hub mode
docs.text:
The stack includes a second backend (db2 / postgrest2) pre-wired at /api2/. Both backends use the Hessen PBF — the importer caches it by filename, so the second import reuses the download.

# In .env: set APP_MODE=hub (and optionally OSM_RELATION_ID / OSM_RELATION_ID2)
make docker-build
make up
make import       # imports Fulda Stadt (454863) into db  — downloads Hessen PBF (~300 MB)
make import2      # imports Neuhof (454881) into db2 — reuses cached PBF

With the bundled seed fixtures instead (fast, no download):

# In .env: set APP_MODE=hub
make up
make seed-load    # 4 Fulda playgrounds  → db
make seed-load2   # 5 Neuhof playgrounds → db2
make docker-build

registry.json (app/public/registry.json) lists both backends (/api = Fulda, /api2 = Neuhof); nginx proxies each to its own PostgREST. Open http://localhost:8080 to see the Hub with two real regions.

The second backend uses OSM_RELATION_ID2 from .env (default 454881 = Neuhof). To test a different second region, set it and re-run make import2.

docs.title: Frontend-only (no database)
docs.text:
When apiBaseUrl is empty in app/public/config.js, the frontend falls back to the Overpass API — no database required for basic frontend work:

make install
make dev

flowchart TD
    browser["Browser"] --> vite["Vite dev server<br/>(hot-reload JS/CSS)"]
    vite --> q{"apiBaseUrl empty?"}
    q -- yes --> overpass["Overpass<br/>(live OSM queries)"]
    q -- no --> postgrest["PostgREST<br/>(Docker stack via make up)"]

To test against the full PostgREST backend instead, start make up and set apiBaseUrl in app/public/config.js.

docs.title: Testing on a phone
docs.text:
make lan-url

Prints your machine's LAN IP and ready-to-use URLs. The Vite dev server and Docker stack both bind to all interfaces, so the printed URLs work immediately on any device on the same WiFi.

Geolocation on mobile

Browsers block the geolocation API on plain HTTP. If you need to test the location button on a phone, use Chrome and enable "Insecure origins treated as secure" at chrome://flags, or test against the production HTTPS URL.

Without make, the same IP comes from:

ip route get 1 | awk '{print $7; exit}'

Then open http://<that-ip>:8080 on your phone.

docs.title: Changes don't appear
docs.text:
Symptom: You edited a JS or CSS file, but the browser still shows the old version.

Fix: Vite hot-reload should pick up changes automatically. If it doesn't:

  1. Check the terminal running make dev — a build error will prevent the browser from updating.
  2. Try a hard reload: Ctrl+Shift+R / Cmd+Shift+R.
  3. If you changed index.html or a file in public/, stop and restart make dev.

When testing against the Docker stack, rebuild and restart the app container after changes:

docker compose up -d --build app   # or: make docker-build

See also the operator troubleshooting page for problems with the Docker stack itself.

docs.text:

  • Build the Poster

docs.title: Maintainer Guide
docs.text: This guide is for maintainers who manage the project's dependencies, toolchain, and release process. It covers how to upgrade key components and how to handle deprecations.

docs.title: Release procedure
docs.text: The checklist lives in RELEASING.md: release commit, tag, then bump main to the next -rc. main always carries the next -rc version between releases.

docs.title: Svelte
docs.text:
Svelte 5 introduced runes (signals-based reactivity). This project currently uses Svelte 5 with legacy writable stores — not runes. Migrating to runes is tracked but not yet done.

To upgrade within Svelte 5:

cd app
npm update svelte @sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte

Run make dev, open the app, and verify: - Map renders and loads playgrounds - Filter panel works - PlaygroundPanel opens on click - Hub mode works (set appMode: 'hub' in public/config.js)

Run make test to confirm E2E tests pass.

For a major version upgrade (Svelte 5 → 6), check the Svelte migration guide first. The migration is likely to involve changes to StandaloneApp.svelte, HubApp.svelte, and all store subscriptions.

docs.title: OpenLayers
docs.text:
cd app
npm update ol

OpenLayers has a history of breaking API changes between minor versions. After upgrading, verify: - Map tiles load - Cluster rings render correctly (clusterStyle.js uses the OL canvas renderer API) - Equipment and polygon layers render - Click handling on playground polygons works - Map.svelte imports — OL occasionally moves modules between paths

docs.title: Tailwind CSS
docs.text:
Tailwind 4 uses a PostCSS plugin (no tailwind.config.js). To upgrade:

cd app
npm update tailwindcss @tailwindcss/postcss

Check that utility classes still apply by opening the app. Tailwind 4's @theme syntax differs from Tailwind 3 — if you see the @ directives breaking, check the Tailwind v4 upgrade guide.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
A PostgreSQL major version (e.g. 16 → 17) cannot read the previous version's data directory, so bumping the image tag is a breaking change for every operator.

  1. Update the PostgreSQL image tag in compose.yml and compose.prod.yml.
  2. Label the PR requires-compose-update and requires-reimport, and say in the release notes that the pgdata volume must be recreated.
  3. Test it on a local stack the way operators will do it: Upgrading → PostgreSQL major version.

docs.title: PostgREST
docs.text:
# compose.yml / compose.prod.yml
image: postgrest/postgrest:v13   # bump this

After upgrading PostgREST: - Run make db-apply — some PostgREST versions change how they interpret SECURITY DEFINER or search_path settings - Verify all /api/rpc/* endpoints work: curl http://localhost:8080/api/rpc/get_meta - Check the PostgREST changelog for breaking changes to the HTTP API or JWT handling

docs.title: osm2pgsql + osmium-tool
docs.text:
These are installed in the importer Docker image (importer/Dockerfile). To upgrade:

  1. Update the apt install versions (or the debian:bookworm-slim base) in importer/Dockerfile
  2. Run make import, which rebuilds the importer image (--build) and imports with it

The importer uses osm2pgsql in default pgsql mode (--slim --drop --hstore) — no Lua script. Check the osm2pgsql changelog for breaking changes to the pgsql output schema or CLI flags when upgrading.

docs.title: Docker base images
docs.text:
The app image (oci/app/Dockerfile) builds the frontend on node:20-alpine and serves it from nginx:alpine. The importer image (importer/Dockerfile) is debian:bookworm-slim with osm2pgsql and osmium-tool from apt.

Update a base image by changing its FROM line and rebuilding:

make docker-build   # rebuilds and restarts the app container only
make import         # rebuilds the importer image and runs an import with it

Then run the tests. The E2E suite builds and serves the frontend itself and stubs the API, so it needs no running stack:

make test

docs.title: Handling deprecations
docs.text:
The codebase currently has one deprecated API: fetchPlaygrounds (region-scoped, replaced by fetchPlaygroundsBbox).

Deprecation process: 1. Add a console.warn in the deprecated function (already done) 2. Add a COMMENT ON FUNCTION in api.sql flagging it for removal 3. Document the planned removal version in the function's JSDoc @deprecated tag 4. Remove in the release after next (one release grace period) 5. Update docs/reference/api.md to mark the function as removed

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text:
When making a significant architectural choice — a new external dependency, a change to the API contract, a new deployment mode — write an ADR in docs/adr/.

File naming: NNNN-short-title.md (e.g. 0002-add-hub-mode.md).

Suggested structure: 

# ADR-NNNN: Title

- **Status:** Proposed | Accepted | Rejected | Superseded
- **Date:** YYYY-MM-DD
- **Deciders:** @username

## Context
What problem are we solving? What are the constraints?

## Decision
What did we decide?

## Alternatives considered
What else did we evaluate and why did we reject it?

## Consequences
What are the positive and negative effects of this decision?

See ADR-0001 for an example. Add the new file to the Develop → Maintain section of nav: in mkdocs.yml, or it does not appear on the site.

docs.title: Dependency audit
docs.text:
Check for outdated or vulnerable packages periodically:

# Frontend
cd app && npm audit && npm outdated

# Root (Playwright)
npm audit && npm outdated

GitHub Dependabot is configured in .github/dependabot.yml and will open PRs for dependency updates automatically.

docs.title: Build the Poster
docs.text:
marketing/poster/ holds a poster for hanging up locally (#1004); how to print it is in the User Guide. This page is about changing and rebuilding it. The poster is a pixel-art scene in the logo's style with a QR code to spieli.eu. One template designed on A5, three languages — poster.html?lang=de|en|sk (default de); the texts are in the TEXT table at the bottom of the file. Open it in a browser to preview.

make poster               # rewrites marketing/poster/print/poster-<lang>-a4.pdf, -2up-a4.pdf and .png

Per language, make poster writes three files:

File What it is poster-<lang>-2up-a4.pdf Two posters on A4 landscape, for handing out. Laid out like the OSM Fulda Aushang sheets: each poster is cut to 137 × 194 mm (the A5 ratio, as large as fits with room for the marks), the two touch in the middle, cut marks sit outside, light hairlines run across the sheet — five cuts. The paper margin is cut away, so a printer's unprintable edge does not matter, and a printer that shrinks the page to about 97 % shrinks the marks with it (sheet.html). poster-<lang>-a4.pdf One poster filling an A4 page (a4.html; A4 and A5 share their ratio, so the design is only scaled). poster-<lang>.png The poster on its own, 150 dpi on A4, for use online. Rendered from the A4 PDF.

Needs a Chromium (CHROME= to point at one), Ghostscript (gs) and network access, because the fonts come from Google Fonts and jsDelivr.

Chromium's PDF is flattened into one opaque 600 dpi image per page. Printers that interpret PDF themselves (e.g. a Brother inkjet over IPP) silently drop images with transparency — every pin — and Type 3 fonts; a flattened page prints the same everywhere. Check a new build with pdfimages -list (no smask rows) and pdffonts (empty).

The files are committed, so anyone can print the poster straight from the repository. After changing the template, run make poster and commit the outputs with it. Only rebuild them for a real change: they add about 5 MB to the history each time.

marketing/poster/preview.png shows all three languages side by side, for the PR and anyone browsing the folder. It is not built by make poster; after a visible change, regenerate it from the PNGs (magick poster-{de,en,sk}.png -resize x900 -bordercolor white -border 20 +append ../preview.png in print/).

When printing, choose actual size / 100 %, not "fit to page". The design keeps a white margin around its frame because inkjets cannot print borderless, and a light sky to save ink. The QR code keeps a white quiet zone of 4 modules (ISO/IEC 18004). Scan the QR code off the printout before hanging it up.

Keep the bubble to things spieli really shows. Shade, for instance, is barely mapped (12 of 473 playgrounds in Landkreis Fulda), so promising it disappoints.

docs.title: Testing Guide
docs.text: spieli has two test layers: unit tests in the frontend and Playwright end-to-end (E2E) tests for the full app.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
make test          # unit tests + Playwright E2E
make test-unit     # unit tests only (fast, no browser)

E2E tests need no Docker stack and no data. Playwright builds the app and serves it with vite preview on http://localhost:4173 (playwright.config.js), and every API response is stubbed in the browser (see Key test helpers).

CI runs both layers automatically on every pull request (e2e.yml + the build-app gate in build.yml).

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Unit tests live next to the module they test, suffixed .test.js, in app/src/lib/, app/src/stores/ and app/src/hub/:

app/src/lib/completeness.test.js
app/src/stores/filters.test.js
app/src/hub/registryEntry.test.js

make test-unit runs npm --prefix app run test:unit, which is an explicit chain of node <file> calls in app/package.json. They are pure Node.js (no bundler, no browser) and run in seconds. One file can be run on its own:

node app/src/lib/completeness.test.js

docs.title: Writing a new unit test
docs.text:
Add a *.test.js file next to the module under test and use node:assert/strict:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { playgroundCompleteness } from './completeness.js';

assert.equal(playgroundCompleteness({ device_count: 1, surface: 'sand' }), 'complete');

Then append it to the test:unit chain in app/package.json; a file that is not in the chain never runs. Tests that import Svelte stores need node --conditions=node …, as the existing store tests show. The Makefile needs no change.

docs.title: Playwright E2E tests
docs.text:
Tests live in tests/, one area of the app per file. Some examples (there are about 40):

File What it tests smoke.spec.js Page load, canvas visible, title tiered.spec.js Cluster/polygon tier RPC selection by zoom selection.spec.js Playground click → panel open, hash written hash-restore.spec.js Deep link restore on page load (#W<osm_id>) hub-smoke.spec.js Hub mode basic page load hub-multi-backend.spec.js Hub fan-out to multiple backends, cross-backend cluster merge hub-deeplink.spec.js Hub deep link with backend slug (#<slug>/W<osm_id>) hub-pill.spec.js Instance pill count display hub-federation-health.spec.js federation-status.json polling and stale banner hub-osm-id-dedup.spec.js Cross-backend duplicate osm_id deduplication cluster-position.spec.js Cluster bucket positions reflect member centroids osmIdDedup.spec.js osmIdDedup logic (unit-style via page evaluate) xss.spec.js Injection safety: OSM tag values rendered as text, not HTML

docs.title: Key test helpers (tests/helpers.js)
docs.text:
The two used by almost every test:

injectApiConfig(page, overrides?)

Intercepts the config.js request and injects a stub window.APP_CONFIG. Default values: apiBaseUrl: '/api', clusterMaxZoom: 0 (polygon-only to keep other suites isolated from the cluster path). Pass overrides to test specific config scenarios:

await injectApiConfig(page, { clusterMaxZoom: 13, mapZoom: 12 });

stubApiRoutes(page)

Intercepts the /api/rpc/* requests the map makes and answers them in the browser: the playground fixture (tests/fixtures/playground.json, or a FeatureCollection you pass) for get_playgrounds* and get_playground, one cluster bucket covering all of them for get_playground_clusters (or the array you pass), and empty results for equipment, trees and POIs. No database or server is involved.

For hub tests, injectHubConfig, stubHubRegistry and stubFederationStatus do the same for the hub's config, registry.json and federation-status.json; makePlayground builds a single fixture feature.

docs.title: Running a single test file
docs.text: npx playwright test tests/smoke.spec.js

docs.title: Running with a UI (headed mode)
docs.text: npx playwright test --ui

docs.title: Updating fixtures
docs.text: There is one static fixture, tests/fixtures/playground.json (a FeatureCollection of playgrounds). Every other response is built in tests/helpers.js or in the test itself. When an API response shape changes (see API reference), update the fixture and the stubs in helpers.js together.

docs.title: Writing a new E2E test
docs.text:
1. Create tests/mynewfeature.spec.js.
  2. Use injectApiConfig and stubApiRoutes in beforeEach to isolate from network + config.
  3. Override specific routes as needed:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { injectApiConfig, stubApiRoutes } from './helpers.js';

test.describe('My feature', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await injectApiConfig(page);
    await stubApiRoutes(page);
  });

  test('does the thing', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    await expect(page.locator('.my-element')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
  1. To test a 404 fallback, override the stubbed route after stubApiRoutes:
await stubApiRoutes(page);
await page.route('**/rpc/get_playground_clusters**', route =>
  route.fulfill({ status: 404, body: '{}' })
);

Playwright processes the most-recently-registered handler first, so the override takes precedence.

docs.title: CI behaviour
docs.text:
Trigger Tests run Pull request against main Build gate + Playwright E2E Push to main Build gate + Playwright E2E Push of v* tag Build gate only (no E2E) — the commit was already tested when it landed on main

Failed E2E runs upload a Playwright HTML report as a CI artefact (30-day retention).

docs.title: Translating spieli
docs.text: Thanks for helping translate spieli! Translation happens on Weblate, which hosts this project free of charge under its Libre plan. This guide explains everything you need to know.

docs.title: What is spieli?
docs.text: spieli is a free, interactive playground map based on OpenStreetMap data. Your translation makes it accessible to communities in your language.

docs.title: How to translate
docs.text:
1. Create a free account on hosted.weblate.org
  2. Open the spieli project, choose the ui-strings component, and pick your language — ui-strings is the one that reaches the app. The project also lists a glossary component; that holds terminology only, and translations made there never ship.
  3. Click any untranslated string and type your translation
  4. Save — that's it. No GitHub account needed.

docs.title: What to translate
docs.text:
Most strings are short UI labels like buttons, tooltips, and status messages:

English Example translation (DE) Show my location Meinen Standort anzeigen Filter Filter Reset all Alle zurücksetzen

docs.title: Things to keep as-is
docs.text:
• Placeholders like {regionName}, {count}, {name} — do not translate these
  • The {count, plural, ...} structure — only translate the text inside the {}

docs.title: Plural forms
docs.text:
Some strings contain a count, like:

{count, plural, one {# bench} other {# benches}}

Keep the {count, plural, ...} wrapper and translate only the text inside. Weblate shows this as a single input field — you must write the complete text, including the {count, plural, …} part with all plural forms for your language.

Languages with two plural forms (German, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Swedish, Portuguese):

{count, plural, one {# Bank} other {# Bänke}}

Languages with no plural forms (Japanese): use other only:

{count, plural, other {# ベンチ}}

Languages with four plural forms (Polish, Ukrainian, Czech, Slovak) — you must include one, few, many, and other.

Careful here: these languages all use four categories, but they disagree about which category a large number lands in. Getting this wrong is easy, because the string still looks complete and Weblate reports no error — it just renders the wrong word for every count from 5 upwards.

Language many matches other matches Polish integers 0 and 5+, except those ending in 2–4 (22 → few; 12–14 stay many) fractions (1.5) Ukrainian integers 0 and 5+, except those ending in 1–4 (21 → one, 22 → few; 11–14 stay many) fractions (1.5) Czech, Slovak fractions (1.5) integers 0 and 5+ (21, 22, 101 all other)

So in Polish and Ukrainian the genitive plural goes in many, and in Czech and Slovak it goes in other.

Polish example — genitive ławek in many, fraction form in other: 

{count, plural, one {# ławka} few {# ławki} many {# ławek} other {# ławki}}

Ukrainian example — genitive лавок in many, fraction form in other: 

{count, plural, one {# лавка} few {# лавки} many {# лавок} other {# лавки}}

Czech example — genitive laviček in other, fraction form in many: 

{count, plural, one {# lavička} few {# lavičky} many {# lavičky} other {# laviček}}

Slovak example — genitive lavičiek in other, fraction form in many: 

{count, plural, one {# lavička} few {# lavičky} many {# lavičky} other {# lavičiek}}

If you are unsure which category your language uses for a given number, check it directly. In any browser's developer console:

new Intl.PluralRules('cs').select(5)   // "other"
new Intl.PluralRules('pl').select(5)   // "many"

This is the same rule the app uses at runtime, so it is authoritative.

Weblate will warn you if the plural structure is broken — fix any flagged strings before saving. It cannot tell you that a grammatically correct form is sitting in the wrong category, so that part is on you.

docs.title: When does my translation go live?
docs.text:
The app currently ships German, English and Slovak. Other languages are collected in Weblate and switched on by a maintainer once they reach 80% completion. That is a manual step: crossing 80% does not switch your language on by itself, but the project's tests then flag it, so it does not get forgotten. Until then your work is saved in the repository and visible to other translators.

A language can also be held back on purpose. French and Spanish currently are (#752): no region on the map serves those languages yet, so they wait until one does. Your work is kept and goes live with it.

If your language has reached 80%, is not held back, and is still not live, open an issue — that is the signal to activate it.

Browsers whose language is not live get the English version. See User Guide → Language.

docs.title: Questions?
docs.text: Open an issue at github.com/mfuhrmann/spieli or leave a comment directly in Weblate.

docs.title: Translation Workflow
docs.text: How translations get into spieli, for developers and maintainers. Translating itself happens on Weblate and needs no GitHub account: see the Translation Guide.

docs.title: Adding new UI strings (developer workflow)
docs.text:
New translatable strings must be added to locales/en.json first. locales/de.json must be updated in the same commit. Adding a key only to de.json breaks Weblate — it uses locales/en.json as the source template and won't surface keys that are absent from it.

Never edit the other locale files by hand. es.json, fr.json, sk.json and the rest are owned by Weblate. Editing one directly collides with whatever a translator has pending for that same file, and Weblate's rebase onto main breaks — which is exactly how the component sat in a merge-conflict error state from May to July 2026, blocking every translation from reaching the repo.

The i18n Guard CI job (.github/workflows/i18n-guard.yml) enforces this: a PR touching any locale other than en.json or de.json fails.

File Who edits it locales/en.json Developers — Weblate's source template locales/de.json Developers — maintainer-authored, primary deployment language everything else Weblate translators only

Two legitimate exceptions bypass the guard:

  • PRs from the weblate-translations branch — Weblate's own translation pushes
  • PRs labelled i18n-manual — landing or repairing a translation out-of-band

Keys follow the existing nested structure. Plural strings use ICU inline format:

"deviceCount": "{count, plural, one {# piece of equipment} other {# pieces of equipment}}"

When you add a new key, Weblate automatically marks it as needing translation in all registered languages.

docs.title: Language graduation
docs.text:
Weblate collects translations for every registered language, but the app loads only the languages listed in SUPPORTED in app/src/lib/i18n.js — today that is de, en and sk. There is no automatic threshold: reaching 100% in Weblate does not by itself make a language visible. Until a maintainer registers it, the locale file sits in the repo and users with that browser language fall back to English.

≥ 80% completion is the bar a maintainer uses to decide a language is ready to activate. When a language crosses it:

  1. Open a PR editing app/src/lib/i18n.js:

    • Add the language code to the SUPPORTED array
    • Add a register() call: register('<lang>', () => import('../../../locales/<lang>.json'));

  2. Title the PR: feat(i18n): add <Language> language support

  3. After merging, the language is live with the next release (locally after make docker-build) for users with that browser language

app/src/lib/i18n.test.js enforces both halves of that: a register() call without a SUPPORTED entry (or the reverse) fails the build, because either on its own is a silent no-op — the locale is simply never selected, with nothing logged. That is how Slovak sat complete and unreachable for weeks (#814).

The same test requires every locale file — registered or not — to parse under intl-messageformat, with the options svelte-i18n uses, and to use only placeholders its English source has (a translated {nombreRegion} is never passed and throws too). A string it cannot parse throws at render rather than degrading, so one bad string breaks whichever view uses it. Until #751 only registered languages were checked, and ten unregistered ones carried 190 i18next-style {{placeholder}} strings unnoticed, so any of them would have needed a repair before it could graduate. Now the Weblate PR that brings in a bad string fails CI: fix the string in Weblate, not in the file, then push from Weblate (Operations → Repository maintenance → Commit, Push; or wlc push) so the PR picks it up. A locked component does not push — check wlc lock-status.

Placeholders take one brace: {regionName}, never {{regionName}}. When repairing them with Weblate's Search and replace, do not replace }} on its own — a plural string legitimately ends in }} (… other {# bancos}}), and a blanket replace breaks every one of them.

The test also asserts the reason each unregistered language is excluded — below 80% key coverage, or a recorded decision not to ship it (DECLINED in the test; es and fr today, since no backend serves those languages, #752) — so any other language that reaches the bar fails the build until someone registers it. The exclusion stays a decision rather than decaying into an oversight.

docs.title: How translations reach the app
docs.text:
Translator edits strings       Weblate pushes commit         Maintainer merges PR
on hosted.weblate.org    →     to weblate-translations   →   into main
  (web UI, no GitHub)           branch on GitHub              → next release image
                                                               → live on instances

Weblate batches translation saves and periodically pushes a commit to the weblate-translations branch, then opens — or reuses — a pull request against main. It keeps one long-lived PR ("Translations update from Hosted Weblate") rather than opening a new one per batch, so the same PR number accumulates commits until a maintainer merges it. The maintainer reviews the JSON diff and merges. Deployed instances get the new strings with the next release image (with Watchtower, within a day of the release); a local checkout sees them after make docker-build.

Weblate never pushes directly to main — every translation update goes through a PR.

Merge that PR with whichever button you like. main allows only squash and rebase merges, and both rewrite Weblate's commits, but the component is set to merge_style: merge so it integrates main by merging rather than by replaying its own commits — see If the component gets stuck.

The live component is spieli/ui-strings. The project also contains an auto-created spieli/glossary component backed by a local-only repository; it holds terminology, has no git remote, and needs no maintenance.

docs.title: If the component gets stuck
docs.text:
Weblate integrates main on every pull. When that integration fails it stays failed — Weblate stops pulling entirely, no translation can reach the repo, and auto_lock_error locks the component. Two distinct causes have hit this project.

1. An upstream commit edited a locale Weblate had pending. Editing fr.json or sk.json by hand collides with whatever a translator has unmerged for that file. The component sat in this state from May to July 2026. The i18n Guard CI job exists to prevent it; see below.

2. A Weblate PR was squash-merged. main is governed by the protect_main ruleset, whose allowed_merge_methods is ["squash", "rebase"] — both rewrite commits, so a Weblate PR can never land with its commits intact and they never become ancestors of main. Under the old merge_style: rebase Weblate replayed all of them on every update, and they conflicted against the already-squashed state:

Rebasing (2/12)
dropping d2359df Translated using Weblate (Czech) -- patch contents already upstream
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in locales/fr.json
error: could not apply 5ed1863... Translated using Weblate (French)

This was structural — it recurred on every Weblate PR merge. Fixed on 2026-07-29 (#794) by switching the component to merge_style: merge, which integrates main by merging instead of replaying. If this cause reappears, check that setting first.

docs.title: Diagnosing
docs.text:
wlc repo reports the component's git state, including the full failure text:

$ wlc repo
merge_failure: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in locales/fr.json
needs_commit: False
needs_merge: True

needs_commit: False means every translator edit in Weblate's database has already been written to its git checkout — so the exported repo you diff below reflects all of their work. If it reads True, run wlc commit first, otherwise that comparison is incomplete before you start. This is not about losing data to the reset: the reset rewrites only Weblate's git checkout, and its database survives (see below).

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Before resetting, prove no translation is lost. Add Weblate's exported repo as a remote and diff every locale against main:

git remote add weblate https://hosted.weblate.org/git/spieli/ui-strings/
git remote update origin weblate
for f in locales/*.json; do
  d=$(git diff --numstat origin/main weblate/main -- "$f")
  [ -n "$d" ] && echo "$f: $d"
done

The weblate URL comes from the component's git_export field and is served by Hosted Weblate natively — there is no Git exporter add-on to enable on this project. Check it resolves before relying on it; without it none of the steps below can be carried out.

A locale that prints nothing is byte-identical on both sides and cannot lose anything. For any locale that does differ, inspect the diff and decide which side is correct — then:

  1. Land anything valuable from Weblate in a normal PR first, labelled i18n-manual, since the reset discards it.
  2. Confirm the salvaged work is merged into main.

  3. Reset Weblate onto upstream:

    wlc lock
wlc reset
wlc pull
wlc unlock

    Run these as four separate commands rather than &&-chained. If reset or pull fails — an API error, a still-conflicting upstream, an expired token — a chain never reaches unlock and leaves translations blocked. If any step fails, run wlc unlock before investigating; wlc lock-status shows where things stand.

    The same four actions exist in the web UI under Operations → Repository maintenance.

  4. Verify: wlc repo shows an empty merge_failure and needs_merge: False, and git remote update weblate leaves weblate/main at the same commit as origin/main.

  5. Close the open "Translations update from Hosted Weblate" PR and delete the weblate-translations branch. A reset only rewrites Weblate's own checkout — anything Weblate already pushed survives it, so that PR still carries the discarded commits and merging it later re-introduces them. Step 4 will not catch this, since it compares only weblate/main against origin/main.

Do not use "Reset and reapply translations" for this — it replays the pending commits onto the reset state and reproduces the same conflict.

A reset touches only Weblate's git checkout. Its database is untouched, so per-string translation history, authorship, suggestions and comments all survive.

docs.title: The wlc CLI
docs.text:
wlc drives the Weblate API from a shell. It is not packaged for Debian or Arch, and PEP 668 blocks pip install --user on most distros:

uv tool install wlc     # or: pipx install wlc

Configure ~/.config/weblate, then chmod 600 it — it holds an API token from your profile:

[weblate]
url = https://hosted.weblate.org/api/
translation = spieli/ui-strings

[keys]
https://hosted.weblate.org/api/ = YOUR_API_KEY
Command Does wlc repo Show git state — merge_failure, needs_commit, needs_merge wlc commit Flush pending translator edits into Weblate's git wlc lock / wlc unlock Block translations while doing repository surgery wlc lock-status Report whether the component is currently locked wlc reset Hard-reset Weblate's checkout onto upstream wlc pull Fetch and integrate main

Lock state is not in wlc show — use wlc lock-status, which reads GET /api/components/spieli/ui-strings/lock/.

docs.title: Weblate component settings
docs.text:
The .weblate.yml file in the repo root records the component configuration. Weblate does not read it — it is a checklist for manual setup and a record of what the live component is set to.
