Many VPS providers (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, etc.) have a separate firewall in their control panel that acts before UFW. If the ACME challenge fails with "connection refused", check that ports 80 and 443 are open there too.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause 502 Bad Gateway spieli stack not running on port 8080 — run docker compose ps from the spieli directory Certificate not issued Port 80 blocked (cloud firewall or UFW), or DNS not yet pointing to this server host.docker.internal not resolved Docker Engine < 20.10 — upgrade Docker Imprint or privacy links open http:// SITE_URL in the spieli .env is set to http://…. Fix it and restart the app container. On a data-node that a hub lists, the hub's links come from the database: also re-apply the schema (run --rm -e API_ONLY=1 importer, see Upgrading) Logs docker compose logs -f from the spieli-traefik/ directory

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
This page is for hub operators. Watching a single data-node or standalone map works differently: see Watching your instance.

The hub container exposes two endpoints for observing federation health:

Endpoint Format Purpose /federation-status.json JSON Human-readable per-backend rollup /metrics Prometheus text Scrape target for Prometheus/Grafana stacks

Both are written atomically every 60 seconds by a cron job inside the hub container. Neither endpoint requires authentication. Cache-Control: no-store is set on both.

Both are described field by field in Hub status and metrics. This page is about using them.

docs.title: Recipe 1 — External uptime monitor
docs.text:
Point any HTTP uptime tool (UptimeRobot, Better Stack, etc.) at:

GET https://<hub-host>/federation-status.json

Check that:

  1. The response is 200 OK.
  2. generated_at is within the last 5 minutes (catches a stopped cron job).
  3. All expected backends.<slug>.up values are true.

docs.title: Recipe 2 — BYO Prometheus + Grafana
docs.text:
Add a scrape job to your prometheus.yml:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: spieli_hub
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['<hub-host>:80']
    metrics_path: /metrics
    scrape_interval: 60s

Useful PromQL expressions:

# Is any backend currently down?
spielplatz_backend_up == 0

# Alert if a daemon-mode backend missed its reimport: REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS
# plus REIMPORT_JITTER_HOURS (default 6) plus time for the import itself.
# Shown for MAX_DAYS=5; one-shot backends (no daemon) only re-import by hand.
spielplatz_backend_data_age_seconds > (5 * 86400 + 6 * 3600 + 3600)

# Alert if the hub poll has stopped writing (cron died)
time() - spielplatz_poll_generated_timestamp > 300

# Detailed share per backend (fraction of playgrounds mapped as detailed)
spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_complete / spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_total

# Playgrounds with no details yet, across all backends
sum(spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_missing)

# Alert if the detailed share drops below 50 % for any backend
spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_complete / spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_total < 0.5

# Which backends are currently importing (data in flux)?
spielplatz_backend_importing == 1

# Backend online but no data and not importing (degraded ring state)
spielplatz_backend_up == 1
  and spielplatz_backend_importing == 0
  and spielplatz_backend_playgrounds_total == 0

docs.title: Recipe 3 — Bundled Prometheus + Grafana dashboard
docs.text:
deploy/monitoring/ is a ready-made stack: Prometheus scraping one hub, and Grafana with the datasource and a spieli federation dashboard provisioned.

cd deploy/monitoring
# point prometheus.yml at your hub (default: a hub-mode stack on this machine, port 8080)
docker compose up -d

Grafana opens at http://127.0.0.1:3001 (read-only, no login), Prometheus at http://127.0.0.1:9091. Both bind to loopback only. Before exposing Grafana anywhere else, turn GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED off in compose.yml and set an admin password.

Keep the job name spieli_hub when changing the target; every panel selects on it. A remote hub needs scheme: https and its host as target — the commented example in prometheus.yml. A standalone stack serves only spielplatz_poll_generated_timestamp, so most panels stay empty against it.

Panel Shows Backends up / down How many backends answered the last get_meta probe Playgrounds (all backends) Sum of playgrounds_total Hub poll age Seconds since the hub last wrote /metrics — high means the poll cron died and every other panel is frozen Up per backend, Importing Per-backend state over time get_meta latency Probe round-trip from the hub server Import age, OSM data age Time since the last import, and age of the OSM extract it imported Detailed share, mapping-detail bars, counts table, totals Playgrounds per backend split into detailed / basic / no details yet

Every panel carries a description (the ⓘ next to its title) of what it shows and what an unusual value means; the data source and the mapping-detail rule are explained once, in the About this dashboard panel at the top.

The dashboard is a provisioned file (grafana/dashboards/federation.json): edits made in the Grafana UI cannot be saved over it. Export the JSON from the UI and replace the file instead.

docs.title: Recipe 4 — Frontend error monitoring
docs.text: spieli ships no frontend error reporting, and adding one needs your own image: see Customise your own image → Frontend error reporting.

docs.text:

  • registry.json reference — backend slug, URL, and metadata fields.
  • API reference — get_meta() response shape including last_import_at.

docs.title: Refreshing OSM Data On Demand
docs.text:
Geofabrik publishes updated OSM extracts daily. The importer pulls the latest extract, filters it to your region, and loads it into the database. This page explains how to trigger that process right now, outside of any automated schedule.

For setting up automatic re-imports, see Scheduled Import.

docs.title: Before you start: know your setup
docs.text:
Check which import mode the installer configured. Run from your deployment directory (where compose.yml and .env live):

grep REIMPORT_INTERVAL .env
Result Mode Both vars absent or empty One-shot — importer runs once and exits Both vars set (e.g. MIN=2, MAX=10) Daemon — importer loops; different steps apply

Check your DEPLOY_MODE too — every command below uses it as <mode>:

grep DEPLOY_MODE .env

Valid values: data-node, data-node-ui. (Hub-only deployments — DEPLOY_MODE=ui — have no database and no importer.)

docs.title: One-shot mode
docs.text:
Run the importer once from your deployment directory. It exits when done.

docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm importer

docs.title: Daemon mode
docs.text:
When REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS and REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS are set, the importer container runs in a loop. On startup it checks last_import_at in the database — if the last import was recent (within a randomly chosen interval), it sleeps until the next scheduled time rather than importing again.

This means restarting the container does not force an immediate re-import unless the data is already overdue. Do not use the one-shot command above here: with the interval variables in .env, run --rm importer starts a second daemon next to the running one.

To force a re-import right now:

Step 1 — Stop the running daemon, so the import is the only writer:

docker compose --profile <mode> stop importer

Step 2 — Run a one-shot import (interval vars unset inline):

docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS= \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS= \
  importer

Unsetting the vars inline overrides .env without editing the file. The container runs once and exits.

Step 3 — Resume the daemon:

docker compose --profile <mode> up -d importer

The daemon restarts, sees the fresh last_import_at, and sleeps for the next scheduled interval.

docs.title: After deleting the database
docs.text: On an empty database (a deleted pgdata volume, down -v, a PostgreSQL major-version upgrade) the daemon imports right away when the stack starts; do not start a second import by hand. In one-shot mode, run the import once as above.

docs.title: Clearing the PBF cache
docs.text:
The importer keeps the downloaded extract and two derived files (the region cut and the tag-filtered extract) in the pbf_cache volume. It checks their timestamps, not their content, so a file left broken by an interrupted or OOM-killed run is reused and the import silently produces 0 playgrounds. Delete the derived files, then run the import as above:

docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm importer \
  sh -c 'rm -f /data/*_${OSM_RELATION_ID}*.pbf*'

The single quotes matter: OSM_RELATION_ID is expanded inside the container, from .env. The source extract stays, so nothing is downloaded again unless Geofabrik has a newer one.

docs.title: Verify the import ran
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/rpc/get_meta | python3 -m json.tool | grep last_import_at

Or from outside the host:

curl -s https://your-domain.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta | python3 -m json.tool | grep last_import_at

last_import_at is when the last import ran. What the other timestamp means: Scheduled Import → How fresh is the data?

docs.title: How long does it take?
docs.text: See Sizing → Import duration.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Scheduled Import — set up automatic re-imports with daemon mode or a systemd timer
  • Monitoring — track import freshness via federation-status.json and Prometheus
  • Upgrading — re-importing after a spieli version upgrade

docs.title: Scheduled Import
docs.text: Geofabrik publishes updated OSM extracts daily. Running the importer on a schedule keeps your playground data fresh without manual intervention.

docs.title: Daemon mode (recommended)
docs.text:
Terminology

"Daemon mode" here refers to the importer container's scheduling behaviour — whether it loops and re-imports automatically or exits after one run. This is separate from DEPLOY_MODE (which services start) and APP_MODE (standalone vs hub frontend).

The importer container has a built-in daemon mode: set REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS and REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS in .env and the container loops forever, re-importing at a random interval within that range. No host cron, no systemd unit — the container manages its own schedule.

REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS=6
REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS=8

A random interval in [MIN, MAX] days is chosen after each successful import, spreading load across operators who deploy at similar times. When the importer container restarts (e.g. after a Watchtower image update), it checks the last import timestamp in the database — if a recent import is on record, it sleeps the remaining interval rather than re-importing immediately.

docs.title: What happens on container startup
docs.text:
Every daemon-mode start runs the same three steps before the schedule takes over:

  1. Apply api.sql — so schema changes carried by a new image take effect at once instead of waiting up to REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS for the next import. Without this a Watchtower update would leave the app on the old schema. Skipped when nothing changed (#971). Every completed apply records two things in public.spieli_schema_apply: a hash of the rendered api.sql (including settings such as PG_WORK_MEM and the legal URLs) and a fingerprint of the live schema (the api functions and the playground_stats definition). A start skips the apply only when both still match, and logs api.sql and the live schema unchanged since the last completed apply — skipping the startup apply. Anything else that touched the schema changes the fingerprint, and the start applies as before: a rollback image, make db-apply of an edited file, or an import killed after osm2pgsql dropped the tables (the record is also cleared before every import). This matters because rebuilding playground_stats is the importer's memory peak: running it on every restart let an upgrade sweep's rebuilds overlap and exhaust a 7.7 GB host.
  2. Grace check — if a recent import is on record, sleep the remainder of the interval instead of re-importing.
  3. Import — otherwise run the import immediately, then loop.

When the daemon is about to be idle for 30 minutes or more it logs [importer] settled — idle for …s. scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh waits for that line, so keep it if you change the log output.

Step 1 is skipped when no import has ever completed. api.sql builds views over the planet_osm_* tables that only exist after the first import, so applying it on a fresh database would fail and restart-loop the container before the import could run. You will see this on a first start:

[importer] No completed import on record — deferring API schema apply to first import.

The import that follows applies the schema itself, so nothing is lost. Both step 1 and step 2 key off the same marker (api.import_status), which is what makes deferring safe: if the marker is absent, the grace check also finds no timestamp and falls straight through to the import. The only wait that can intervene is the deliberate fresh-install stagger (REIMPORT_STARTUP_JITTER_MAX_HOURS) — never a grace sleep.

If the importer cannot reach the database to answer that question, it retries, then says so and continues to the import rather than assuming either answer:

[importer] WARNING: import state unknown after 3 attempts — skipping startup API schema apply and continuing to import.

Seeing that line on a populated node means credentials or connectivity need attention — see Troubleshooting.

When both vars are unset (default)

The importer runs once and exits (one-shot mode). Use this when you manage scheduling externally (systemd, cron).

docs.title: Enabling daemon mode
docs.text:
Add the two vars to .env:

REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS=6
REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS=8

Then recreate the importer so it picks up the new env (restart would keep the old container and its old environment):

docker compose --profile data-node-ui up -d importer

Check that it entered daemon mode:

docker compose logs importer | grep -i daemon
# [importer] Daemon mode: interval 6–8 days, jitter up to 6h.

docs.title: Keeping stacks from importing at the same time
docs.text:
Several stacks on one host must not run osm2pgsql together — it is the memory peak of the whole pipeline. Two mechanisms spread them out (#882):

  • REIMPORT_JITTER_HOURS (default 6) adds a random 0–6 h to every scheduled wait, and delays an import that is already overdue at startup by the same amount — but never past MAX_DAYS plus one jitter window after the last import, so frequent restarts cannot keep postponing it. Without it, a restart of every stack (an upgrade sweep, a host reboot) stamped all overdue stacks with nearly the same last_import_at; with MIN == MAX each stack then only moved by its own import duration, so stacks with similar import times kept their shared slot. With it, slots drift apart every cycle. Set it to 0 only if a single stack runs on the host.

    Jitter makes overlap unlikely, not impossible: there is no lock between stacks on one host (tracked in #961). - REIMPORT_STARTUP_JITTER_MAX_HOURS (default 0) staggers the first import on a fresh database, for deploying many stacks at once.

Both draw from /dev/urandom. Before #882 they were seeded from the clock's current second, so containers started together drew the same "random" value. Values that are not whole numbers are replaced by the default with a warning in the importer log, as is MIN > MAX (swapped).

Every wait logs the absolute time of the next run, so the spread on a host is one loop away:

for d in ~/spieli-*; do
  printf '%-28s ' "$(basename "$d")"
  docker compose --project-directory "$d" logs importer 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -o 'next run at .*' | tail -n 1
done

docs.title: Automatic image updates with Watchtower
docs.text: Watchtower complements daemon mode: it installs new spieli images once a day, and the startup grace check above keeps those restarts from triggering an unplanned re-import. How to enable it and what it does: Upgrading → Automatic upgrade.

docs.title: How long does an import take?
docs.text: See Sizing → Import duration.

docs.title: How fresh is the data?
docs.text:
Geofabrik refreshes most regional extracts daily. The importer stores two timestamps in the database:

  • last_import_at — when the importer script ran (visible via GET /api/rpc/get_meta)
  • osm_data_timestamp — the osmosis_replication_timestamp header from the source PBF, which reflects when Geofabrik generated that extract (can be up to a week old for less-trafficked regions)

Both are surfaced in Monitoring → /federation-status.json.

docs.title: Without daemon mode (host-managed scheduling)
docs.text: If you prefer external scheduling, leave REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS and REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS unset. The importer exits with code 0 after a successful one-shot run.

docs.title: systemd timer
docs.text:
spieli ships unit files in the repository's deploy/ directory for Linux hosts with systemd. The installer does not download them; fetch them for your release:

TAG=vX.Y.Z   # the release you run (docker compose images shows it)
RAW=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mfuhrmann/spieli/${TAG}/deploy
sudo curl -fsSL "$RAW/spieli-import.service" -o /etc/systemd/system/spieli-import.service
sudo curl -fsSL "$RAW/spieli-import.timer"   -o /etc/systemd/system/spieli-import.timer

Open /etc/systemd/system/spieli-import.service and set:

  • WorkingDirectory= — directory where compose.yml and .env live (e.g. /opt/spieli)
  • EnvironmentFile= — path to .env (usually WorkingDirectory/.env)
  • User= — add it, set to a user in the docker group that owns the deployment directory (the shipped unit has none, so it runs as root)

The shipped timer uses OnCalendar=weekly, which systemd reads as Monday 00:00, with Persistent=true so a run missed while the host was off happens at the next boot. Change the schedule in spieli-import.timer, for example:

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Sun 04:00      # weekly, Sunday 4 AM
# OnCalendar=daily         # every day at midnight
# OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:30  # every day at 3:30 AM

Enable and start:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now spieli-import.timer
systemctl list-timers spieli-import.timer

docs.title: Host cron
docs.text: 0 4 * * 0 cd /opt/spieli && docker compose --profile data-node-ui run --rm importer >> /var/log/spieli-import.log 2>&1

docs.title: Security Hardening
docs.text: This page covers steps to harden a spieli deployment for production. The default configuration is designed for getting started quickly — some defaults should be changed before exposing an instance to the internet.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Change the database password
  • [ ] Enable HTTPS with a reverse proxy
  • [ ] Restrict database network exposure
  • [ ] Review nginx security headers
  • [ ] Keep images up to date

docs.title: Database password
docs.text:
The installer generates a random password for you. If you set the stack up by hand, the default in .env.example is change-me; set a strong random one before starting the stack for the first time:

openssl rand -hex 32   # what the installer uses

Use hex rather than base64: the password ends up in a PostgreSQL connection URI, and the +, / and = that base64 produces break it.

Edit .env:

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-generated-password

The password is used only internally between PostgREST and PostgreSQL — it never leaves the Docker network. Still, a default password is a risk if the database port is accidentally exposed.

docs.title: HTTPS with a reverse proxy
docs.text:
The Docker stack listens on plain HTTP (port APP_PORT, default 8080). In production, put an HTTPS-terminating reverse proxy in front of it. The bundled Traefik installer does this with Let's Encrypt, including renewal: HTTPS setup.

Any other reverse proxy works too. With Caddy, which obtains certificates by itself:

playground.example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8080
}

docs.title: Restrict database port exposure
docs.text:
The compose.yml does not publish the PostgreSQL or PostgREST ports to the host — only the app container's APP_PORT is published. Verify with:

docker compose ps

The db and postgrest services should show no host port bindings. If you see 0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp, your database is accessible from the network. Remove the ports: entry for the db service from your compose file.

docs.title: nginx security headers
docs.text:
The bundled oci/app/nginx.conf sets several security headers:

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(self)

The Content Security Policy is generated at container startup by oci/app/docker-entrypoint.sh into /etc/nginx/csp.conf, which nginx.conf includes. It is not a literal, because two parts of the correct policy are only knowable at runtime: in hub mode the browser connects to backends listed in an operator-supplied registry.json, and a basemap opt-out puts a third-party tile host back in the browser. A literal wide enough for every deployment is a literal that protects none of them.

To see the policy your instance actually serves:

docker compose exec app cat /etc/nginx/csp.conf

docs.title: Two policies ship together, on purpose
docs.text:
During the current release the container sends both of these:

Header Host lists Status Content-Security-Policy img-src/connect-src still https: Enforced Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only narrowed to the hosts actually used Observed only

The narrowed policy is delivered in report-only form first because the failure mode of an over-tight CSP is silent: photos simply do not appear, with nothing but a browser console message. So the first breakage would show up in production, on a rarely used path. Once testing in both app modes and both basemap setups shows no violations in the browser console, the report-only policy becomes the enforced one and the wildcard policy is deleted.

If you see console messages beginning Content Security Policy while running this release, nothing is being blocked — but please report them, because they are exactly what the observation period is for.

There is deliberately no report-uri. It would collect a per-visitor record of what each browser tried to load, on your disk, which is the same shape of trail that serving the basemap yourself exists to remove.

docs.title: What the narrowed policy allows, and why
docs.text:
• img-src 'self' data: https://api.panoramax.xyz — with every proxy on, Panoramax thumbnails are the only images the browser still fetches from a third party: the endpoint redirects to a per-instance derivative host nginx cannot follow. Narrowing that away would block the thumbnails and put a false statement on the privacy page. With PROXY_COMMONS=false, the Wikimedia and OSM-wiki hosts are added (https://*.wikimedia.org https://wikimedia.org https://*.wikipedia.org https://wikipedia.org https://wiki.openstreetmap.org). The Wikimedia entries are wildcards because app/src/lib/commons.js accepts an OSM image tag on any of those hosts; pinning it to upload. and commons. would silently stop rendering valid tags, and which host serves a file is not fixed — the API currently returns thumbnails on thumb.wikimedia.org. The apex domains are listed separately because *.example.org does not match example.org in CSP.
  • connect-src 'self' — in a default deployment, nothing more. Since the external services are fetched server-side (see External-service proxies), the browser has nothing third-party to connect to. Opting a proxy out with PROXY_NOMINATIM=false and friends adds that service's host back. Three further origins are added automatically when your configuration calls for them:
    • A remote API_BASE_URL. A DEPLOY_MODE=ui stack points at PostgREST on another host, and every data call goes to ${API_BASE_URL}/rpc/…. Its origin is added, scheme and port included.
    • Your hub backends. Read from the url fields of registry.json when the registry is a same-origin file the entrypoint can read. Only url values are used — a website or docs link elsewhere in the registry does not widen the policy. If your registry is fetched from a URL at runtime, use CSP_CONNECT_EXTRA.
    • Your basemap host, if you opted out of same-origin delivery.
  • frame-src https://panoramax.xyz https://api.panoramax.xyz — the street-level photo viewer. Already narrow, and the model the rest of the policy now follows.
  • frame-ancestors 'self' https: — still a wildcard, deliberately. It governs who may embed spieli, not what spieli discloses, and a hub embeds standalone instances.

Why narrow img-src and connect-src at all, when every service above is wanted? Because the values that reach the URL builders come from OSM tags, which are arbitrary attacker-editable strings. commons.js validates that an image tag points at a Wikimedia host before rendering it, and with a https: wildcard that code check is the only thing between a crafted tag and a visitor's browser fetching from a host of the tagger's choosing. The policy is the second line behind that check. Both are tested: tests/hostile-image-tag.spec.js covers the code check, and the CSP must follow the configuration CI job covers the generated policy.

docs.title: Escape hatches
docs.text:
Two variables add origins the generator cannot discover. Both take a space-separated list of hosts or origins, and both reject a malformed value at startup rather than emitting a policy that blocks the origin it was meant to allow.

Variable Adds to Use when CSP_CONNECT_EXTRA connect-src Your hub fetches registry.json from a URL at runtime, so the entrypoint cannot read it to discover backends CSP_IMG_EXTRA img-src You render images from an origin the generator does not know about

A self-hosted tileserver does not need either of these, whatever port or scheme it uses: the basemap host is derived as a full origin, scheme and port intact, precisely because a CSP host-source with no port matches only the scheme's default port and one with no scheme matches only the document's own scheme. The privacy page's service table still shows the bare host, which is what reads well there.

docs.title: External service dependencies
docs.text:
By default spieli calls third-party services from the server, not from the visitor's browser: search, photos, reviews and the background map are fetched through same-origin paths and cached. Only Panoramax (thumbnails, and the viewer once a visitor opens it) and OpenStreetMap notes (when a visitor sends a hint) are contacted by the browser directly. Why, and what that does and does not protect: Privacy by design. Every service and its path: External Services.

What matters for hardening is that the default is a setting you can leave. Opting any PROXY_* variable out, or pointing BASEMAP_URL / BASEMAP_STYLE_URL at a third party, moves that service back into the browser. The generated Content Security Policy (above) and the generated privacy page both follow that choice automatically, so neither has to be edited by hand. Settings: Basemap and external services.

docs.title: CORS for Hub data-nodes
docs.text: Data-nodes (data-node-ui mode) respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on all /api/ endpoints. This is intentional — the Hub's browser must be able to query data-nodes cross-origin. Restricting it to specific hub origins needs your own image: see Customise your own image → Restrict CORS.

docs.title: Keeping images up to date
docs.text:
Two ways, both fine:

  • Automatically (the installer's default): the auto-update profile runs Watchtower, which installs new releases within a day. See Upgrading → Automatic upgrade.

  • By hand: pin a version in compose.yml for both images and upgrade deliberately, following Upgrading:

    image: ghcr.io/mfuhrmann/spieli:0.14.0
image: ghcr.io/mfuhrmann/spieli-importer:0.14.0

Either way, subscribe to GitHub Releases: releases with a breaking label need a manual step even with Watchtower.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration reference — POSTGRES_PASSWORD and all env vars
  • Upgrading — how to update to a new release
  • Monitoring — observability for production instances

docs.title: Shared basemap cache
docs.text: This page is only for hosts running several spieli stacks. A single-stack operator needs nothing here: every instance already caches basemap tiles on its own, and that is the shipped default.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Each stack fetches tiles from BASEMAP_UPSTREAM and caches them itself. That is the right default — it is portable and needs no extra component — but on a host with many stacks it multiplies:

Per-stack caches (default) One shared cache Disk at the 4 GB default × 15 stacks up to 60 GB one cache, sized once Clients the tile server sees 15 1 Cold starts after an upgrade sweep 15, all at once none — the cache outlives the stacks

The last row is the one that matters most. scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh walks the stacks in sequence, and without a shared cache each one comes back empty and refills from the public tile server. Fifteen cold caches hitting a donation-funded server run by one person, in a burst, is the load pattern this whole design exists to avoid.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The visitor's browser never touches the shared cache. It only ever talks to its own stack's nginx, which fetches through the cache server-side:

browser ──► stack nginx ──► shared cache ──► tiles.openfreemap.org
            (per domain)     (one per host)   (one client for the host)
             /basemap/

This is why the shared cache needs no Traefik router, no CORS exception and no CSP allowance, and why the same-origin privacy property is preserved for free: as far as the browser is concerned nothing changed.

One rewrite is load-bearing

The TileJSON document a tileserver returns carries absolute tile URLs pointing at itself. The shared cache rewrites those to the relative path /basemap/, which is correct for every stack regardless of its domain, because it is a path and not a host.

Without that rewrite each stack would look for its configured upstream — now the cache, not the provider — find nothing to rewrite, and hand the browser tiles.openfreemap.org URLs directly. The map would still render perfectly while quietly undoing the same-origin property. CI asserts the rewrite for this reason.

docs.title: 0. Get the files
docs.text:
The installer does not download these. From a clone, they are deploy/basemap-cache/ and compose.override.basemap-cache.yml in the repository root. On an installed host, fetch them for the release you run (the same TAG as in the Quick Start):

TAG=vX.Y.Z   # the release you run (docker compose images shows it)
RAW=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mfuhrmann/spieli/${TAG}
mkdir -p deploy/basemap-cache
curl -fsSL "$RAW/deploy/basemap-cache/compose.yml"         -o deploy/basemap-cache/compose.yml
curl -fsSL "$RAW/deploy/basemap-cache/nginx.conf.template" -o deploy/basemap-cache/nginx.conf.template
# and into every stack's directory, next to its compose.yml:
curl -fsSL "$RAW/compose.override.basemap-cache.yml" -o compose.override.basemap-cache.yml

docs.title: 1. Start the cache
docs.text:
It creates the spieli-basemap network the stacks join, so it goes up first.

cd deploy/basemap-cache
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps

Defaults are sized for a shared cache rather than fifteen small ones: 16 GB, a 128 MB keys_zone, and a 180-day inactive. Override in a .env next to that compose file if the host has different headroom.

keys_zone holds roughly 8,000 keys per MB and binds before disk does, so keep the two in step. A large max_size behind a small zone yields a cache that stays almost empty.

Set a real BASEMAP_CACHE_UA. This container is the single client the tile server sees for the whole host, so it is the one that has to identify a contactable operator:

BASEMAP_CACHE_UA='spieli/shared-basemap-cache (+https://spieli.eu; ops@example.org)'

docs.title: 2. Point each stack at it
docs.text:
In every stack's .env:

BASEMAP_UPSTREAM=http://basemap-cache
BASEMAP_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=256m

The second line matters. The per-stack cache does not disappear — it becomes a small L1 in front of the shared L2. Leaving it at the 4 GB default across fifteen stacks spends 60 GB to save a sub-millisecond hop on the same host.

Then start each stack with the override that joins the network:

docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.override.basemap-cache.yml up -d

To make that permanent, set it once per stack instead of typing it each time:

echo 'COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yml:compose.override.basemap-cache.yml' >> .env

scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh runs plain docker compose commands, so it picks COMPOSE_FILE up automatically and no change to the script is needed.

docs.title: 3. Check it is actually being used
docs.text:
# The cache should report hits, not misses, once warm
docker compose -f deploy/basemap-cache/compose.yml exec basemap-cache \
  wget -qS -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/planet 2>&1 | grep -i x-basemap-cache

A stack is wired up correctly when its TileJSON names same-origin tiles:

curl -s http://localhost:8081/basemap/planet | head -c 120
# {"tilejson":"3.0.0","tiles":["/basemap/planet/<build>/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"],…

If that shows an absolute https://… URL instead, the stack is not going through the shared cache, or the cache's BASEMAP_UPSTREAM_HOST does not match the provider it actually fetches from.

docs.title: Access logging
docs.text:
The cache sets access_log off on tile requests, for the same reason each stack does: at high zoom the z/x/y stream is not metadata about what someone looked at, it is what they looked at. Moving that stream onto the operator's own server and then logging it would be worse than the third-party delivery it replaces.

error_log still records a failing URI, which is what keeps outages diagnosable.

Traefik never sees basemap traffic in this topology — the browser fetches tiles from its own stack, and the stack reaches the cache over an internal Docker network — so there is nothing to exclude at the ingress. Traefik's access log is off by default in deploy/traefik/; if you enable it for other reasons, that remains true only as long as tiles do not start flowing through it.

docs.title: Exposure
docs.text:
Nothing is published. The cache listens only on the spieli-basemap Docker network, so it is not reachable from outside the host at all.

It still constrains what it will fetch — an asset-shaped path, GET only, no query strings — even though every request comes from a stack that has already applied the same rule. A caching proxy that will fetch arbitrary paths is a relay someone else can fill on your behalf, and defence in depth is cheap here.

docs.title: Running your own tileserver instead
docs.text:
The same variable does both jobs. Point the shared cache at your own server rather than the public one:

# deploy/basemap-cache/.env
BASEMAP_UPSTREAM=http://tileserver:8080
BASEMAP_UPSTREAM_HOST=tileserver:8080

If that server's URL layout differs from the provider's, the bundled style needs rebuilding against it too — see Customise your own image → Your own tileserver. The stacks need no change either way.

docs.title: Single-host Federation
docs.text: A single-host federation runs a pure hub (no database) and multiple regional data-nodes on one VPS. It is a valid alternative to the distributed topology and suits operators who want full-country coverage without coordinating multiple machines.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph vps["one VPS"]
        hub["spieli (hub)<br/>DEPLOY_MODE=ui<br/>port 8080"]
        hessen["spieli-hessen<br/>data-node-ui<br/>port 8081"]
        berlin["spieli-berlin<br/>data-node-ui<br/>port 8082"]
        more["spieli-nrw …<br/>data-node-ui<br/>port 8088"]
    end
    browser["Browser"]
    browser --> hub
    browser --> hessen
    browser --> berlin
    browser --> more

The hub serves the frontend and registry.json. Browsers fetch playground data cross-origin from each data-node's /api/. The hub itself has no database and no importer.

docs.title: When to use this topology
docs.text:
• One operator wants to cover a large region (e.g. all of Germany) without a multi-hour single import.
  • You want a live test bed for hub federation features.
  • You don't (yet) have other operators to host regional backends.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Resource Minimum Recommended RAM 6 GiB 8 GiB Swap 4 GiB 4 GiB Disk 20 GiB 40 GiB+

Swap is required. Without swap, the Linux OOM killer fires when multiple importers run near-simultaneously, killing whichever process is largest at that moment. Even if each individual import fits in RAM, two medium-sized backends starting at the same time can exhaust available memory. 4 GiB of swap gives the kernel room to page out idle data and survive the overlap.

sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

docs.title: Per-backend RAM and disk
docs.text: See Sizing: measured memory and disk per region class, and what an import needs on top. Plan for the sum of the serving memory plus one import at a time, which is why imports must not overlap (see swap above and Scheduled Import).

docs.title: Port allocation
docs.text:
Stack Port Profile(s) Hub 8080 ui auto-update First data-node (e.g. Hessen) 8081 data-node-ui Second data-node (e.g. Berlin) 8082 data-node-ui … 8083–8096 data-node-ui

Use consecutive ports and unique COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME per stack.

docs.title: Hub
docs.text:
The hub runs DEPLOY_MODE=ui with no database. Its .env contains no OSM_RELATION_ID, PBF_URL, or POSTGRES_PASSWORD:

COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=spieli
DEPLOY_MODE=ui
APP_MODE=hub
APP_PORT=8080
REGISTRY_URL=/registry.json
HUB_POLL_INTERVAL=300
SITE_URL=https://hub.example.com
IMPRESSUM_NAME=...
IMPRESSUM_ADDRESS=...
IMPRESSUM_EMAIL=...

Bind-mount registry.json via compose.override.yml so you can update it without rebuilding:

services:
  app:
    volumes:
      - ./registry.json:/usr/share/nginx/html/registry.json:ro

Start with --profile ui --profile auto-update (Watchtower lives here and covers all containers on the host):

docker compose --profile ui --profile auto-update up -d

docs.title: Data-nodes
docs.text:
Use scripts/setup-germany-backends.sh as a starting point for bulk setup. Edit the SKIP_SLUGS array for backends hosted elsewhere or not yet ready, and set DOMAIN_SUFFIX and TRAEFIK_DYNAMIC_DIR to match your environment.

For each backend the script creates the directory, patches compose.yml, writes .env, and drops a Traefik dynamic config. It does not start imports — do those manually after checking RAM.

docs.title: First import — one-shot before daemon
docs.text:
On a fresh database the daemon imports right away (after REIMPORT_STARTUP_JITTER_MAX_HOURS, if set); it defers the schema apply until that first import has finished (#759). On a shared host, though, you want to decide when each first import runs, so that two large ones never overlap. So run the first import as a one-shot (no daemon env vars), then start the daemon:

cd ~/spieli-<slug>

# 1. Start db, postgrest, app — but not importer
docker compose --profile data-node-ui up -d db postgrest app

# 2. Run one-shot import (overrides daemon env vars from .env)
docker compose --profile data-node-ui run --rm \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS= \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS= \
  -e REIMPORT_STARTUP_JITTER_MAX_HOURS= \
  importer

# 3. After success, start daemon
docker compose --profile data-node-ui up -d importer

Import large backends one at a time. Check free -h before each large one.

docs.title: Keeping imports apart
docs.text:
Two settings spread the imports of stacks that share a host:

  • REIMPORT_JITTER_HOURS (default 6) adds a random 0–N hours to every scheduled wait, and to an import that is already overdue when the container starts. Stacks that once imported together (after an upgrade sweep or a reboot) drift apart instead of keeping a shared slot (#882).
  • REIMPORT_STARTUP_JITTER_MAX_HOURS (default 0) delays only the first import on a fresh database by a random amount, so backends set up at the same time do not all import at once. It has no effect once a backend has data, so set it before the first start, not afterwards.

Neither rules out an overlap; two imports can still land close together, which is why swap is required. See Scheduled Import → Keeping stacks from importing at the same time.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
When the hub and its data-nodes share a single VPS, use scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh. It handles the correct order (data-nodes first, hub last) and runs each stack sequentially to avoid OOM from concurrent importer runs.

Copy the script to the VPS once, then edit the STACKS array to match your port layout:

scp scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh user@vps:~/upgrade-stacks.sh

STACKS=(
  "$HOME/spieli-hessen:data-node-ui:8081"
  "$HOME/spieli-berlin:data-node-ui:8082"
  "$HOME/spieli:ui auto-update:8080"   # hub last
)

Run:

bash ~/upgrade-stacks.sh

Per stack, in this order — the order is the point:

  1. Pull images.
  2. Stop the daemon importer (data-nodes only), so it cannot race the schema apply. The manual procedure says this step is not optional; the script does it for you.
  3. Apply api.sql via a one-shot API_ONLY=1 importer, which never triggers a full reimport. If it fails, the daemon importer is brought back up before the sweep aborts, so a failed run never leaves a stack with its importer stopped.
  4. Recreate the daemon importer with up -d --force-recreate. The plain restart form is what left daemons running the old image during the v0.9.0 sweep.
  5. Restart the app container — last, so it never serves against a schema the database does not have yet.
  6. Verify by polling get_meta for up to 180 s, treating only 200 and 404 as settled. Verifying before step 4 is precisely what made #800 invisible: the old schema is internally consistent enough to pass.

The hub entry skips steps 2–4 automatically.

The sweep runs one heavy job at a time (#971). After a data-node's app is restarted and verified, the sweep waits until its importer logs [importer] settled — no schema rebuild or import running or imminent — before touching the next stack; a stack that was mid-import waits for that import to end, and the zero-playground safety-net reimport now runs in the foreground. It waits up to SETTLE_TIMEOUT_MIN (default 120) minutes per stack, then stops rather than overlap two stacks. Before, it moved on as soon as get_meta answered, which it does at once because the old view keeps serving during a rebuild; during the v0.12.0 sweep two stacks' rebuilds overlapped and the host ran out of memory. Combined with the daemon skipping an unchanged startup apply, a sweep of already-current stacks does no rebuild at all.

A sweep restarts every import clock. Recreating the daemon importer runs its startup grace check, and every stack whose import is overdue imports right then. Since #882 each such import first waits a random 0–REIMPORT_JITTER_HOURS (default 6 h), so a sweep no longer stamps all of them into one window — but on a memory-constrained host it is still worth checking the spread afterwards (see Keeping imports apart).

A stack that is mid-import is skipped, not forced. If get_meta reports importing: true, the script leaves the schema alone and says so: stopping the importer there would SIGKILL osm2pgsql after 10 s and leave the database partially imported. The app is still upgraded, and the stack is listed separately at the end — re-run the sweep for it once the import has finished.

The script does not touch .env or compose.yml. A release labelled requires-env-update or requires-compose-update needs those applied to every stack before the sweep. It is easy to miss, because the script otherwise looks like the whole federation procedure.

Verification is not fatal to the sweep. By the time a stack is verified its images are already pulled and its containers restarted, so a failed check means the upgrade worked but the stack is not serving data yet. The script records the stack, carries on with the rest, and exits non-zero at the end listing every inconclusive one. A data-node that has never completed an import answers 404 on get_meta and is called out as such — expected until its first import finishes.

If the sweep does abort — a failed image pull or container start — it prints which stacks were upgraded, which one it stopped on, and that everything from there onward was not reached. Completed stacks are idempotent, so re-run after fixing the cause. One caveat it will warn you about: if a forced reimport was launched in the background before the abort, wait for it to finish first, or the next run's API_ONLY=1 step races it on the playground_stats rebuild.

Standard releases with Watchtower active need no sweep — the daemon importer applies a changed api.sql when it restarts (an unchanged one is skipped, #971). Only breaking-label releases need manual steps.

docs.title: Watchtower
docs.text: Only the hub stack runs --profile auto-update; its Watchtower updates every stack on the host. Why: Upgrading → One Watchtower per host.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Federated Deployment — distributed (multi-host) topology
  • Add a Data-node — adding one backend at a time
  • Upgrading — full upgrade guide for all deployment types
  • Configuration reference — all env vars

docs.title: Switching regions
docs.text:
This guide covers changing the geographic coverage of a running spieli instance — for example, switching from a district to a whole state, or expanding to all of Germany.

The process requires a full database re-import. Plan for downtime proportional to the size of the new extract (see Import duration).

docs.title: 1. Find the new relation ID and PBF extract
docs.text:
OSM relation ID — search on Nominatim. The relation ID appears in the URL: openstreetmap.org/relation/51477 → ID is 51477.

PBF extract — browse download.geofabrik.de for an extract that covers your target region. The extract only needs to contain your region — a country extract works fine for a single state.

Common extracts:

Coverage URL Germany https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany-latest.osm.pbf Baden-Württemberg https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany/baden-wuerttemberg-latest.osm.pbf Bayern https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany/bayern-latest.osm.pbf Hessen https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany/hessen-latest.osm.pbf NRW https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany/nordrhein-westfalen-latest.osm.pbf

docs.title: 2. Update .env
docs.text:
Edit ~/spieli/.env and change the two region-specific lines:

OSM_RELATION_ID=51477
PBF_URL=https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany-latest.osm.pbf

docs.title: 3. Wipe the database and re-import
docs.text:
Warning: This permanently deletes all existing playground data. The import re-downloads the PBF and rebuilds the database from scratch.

cd ~/spieli

# Stop the stack
docker compose --profile data-node-ui down

# Delete the database and cached PBF
# (the prefix is the compose project name — the directory name unless COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME is set;
#  `docker volume ls` shows the exact names)
docker volume rm spieli_pgdata spieli_pbf_cache

# Start the stack (initialises a fresh database)
docker compose --profile data-node-ui up -d

Then start the import, depending on how the stack runs:

  • With automatic updates (daemon mode, REIMPORT_INTERVAL_* set in .env): nothing to do. On an empty database the daemon starts the import by itself. Running the importer by hand as well would start a second import alongside it. Follow it with docker compose logs -f importer.

  • Without automatic updates: run it once:

    docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm importer

The app will return empty responses until the import finishes.

docs.title: Import duration
docs.text: See Sizing → Import duration.

docs.title: After the import
docs.text:
The app picks up the new data automatically — no restart needed. Verify with:

curl -s https://yourdomain.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta | python3 -m json.tool

The playground_count and bbox fields should reflect the new region.

docs.title: A stack serves the old schema after an upgrade
docs.text:
Symptom: Nothing looks wrong. get_meta answers, row counts are plausible, the UI loads — but a filter added in the new release returns nothing, or returns the pre-release answer.

Cause: Two sessions applied api.sql around the same time, and the one that finished last came from the older image. The daemon importer applies the schema on container startup, so any restart of it during an upgrade makes it a second writer; and a plain docker compose up -d importer restarts the existing container rather than recreating it, so that writer is still running the previous image. The old schema is internally consistent, so every health check passes (#800).

This is what happened during the v0.9.0 upgrade sweep: a stack ran the v0.9.0 app against the v0.8.0 playground_stats view, with has_theme missing and has_fence still matching barrier=fence only.

Diagnose by comparing the version get_meta reports against the release you installed:

curl -sf http://localhost:<port>/api/rpc/get_meta | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['version'])"

That field comes from the image that last applied api.sql, which is exactly the question. Do not check for the presence of a column instead: a column added in an earlier release exists in both schemas, so the check passes on the old one.

Fix by recreating the daemon importer on the new image, then re-checking:

docker compose --profile <mode> up -d --force-recreate importer
docker compose logs -f importer   # wait for "Done. PostgREST schema reloaded."

--force-recreate is the point: a plain up -d restarts the container from the image it was created with.

Prevention. From v0.10.0 api.sql takes a session-level advisory lock, so concurrent applies queue instead of corrupting each other, and scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh stops the importer before applying and recreates it afterwards. The lock cannot tell an old image from a new one, though — it prevents corruption, not a stale last writer — so the stop/recreate ordering still matters when upgrading by hand. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Schema apply fails with relation "public.playground_stats" does not exist
docs.text:
Symptom: An API_ONLY=1 run dies partway through:

psql:/tmp/tmp.XXXXXX:352: ERROR:  relation "public.playground_stats" does not exist

Cause: Two concurrent applies, as above — on v0.9.0 and earlier, where api.sql dropped the matview and rebuilt it in place, so the second session's DROP removed it while the first was still indexing.

This should no longer happen. From v0.10.0 the rebuild builds under a staging name and swaps it in (#720), and the advisory lock serialises applies (#800). If you still see it, check whether something is applying an older api.sql — a stack that has not been upgraded, or an importer container still on a previous image.

Recovery on v0.9.0 and earlier: re-run API_ONLY=1. If the matview is gone entirely, a full re-import recreates everything.

docs.title: Port 8080 is already in use
docs.text:
Symptom: docker compose up fails with address already in use or port is already allocated.

Fix: Stop whatever is using port 8080, or change the port in .env:

APP_PORT=8081

Then restart the stack:

docker compose -f compose.yml --profile <mode> up -d

docs.title: Import exits immediately or fails with a database error
docs.text:
Symptom: The import finishes in seconds (normally takes minutes), or you see a connection refused or role does not exist error.

Fix: The database must be running before you import. Start the stack first and confirm all containers are healthy:

docker compose ps   # all containers should show "running" or "healthy"

Then start the import (Refresh Data). If the database shows as unhealthy, try stopping and restarting the stack.

docs.title: Importer restart-loops on a fresh install with relation "planet_osm_point" does not exist
docs.text:
Symptom: On a brand-new data-node install the importer never populates the database and restarts forever:

importer-1  | [importer] Daemon mode: interval 2–10 days, jitter up to 6h.
importer-1  | [importer] API_ONLY mode — skipping PBF download and osm2pgsql import.
importer-1  | [importer] Applying API schema...
importer-1  | psql:/tmp/tmp.JsTPhaBgfJ:87: ERROR:  relation "planet_osm_point" does not exist
importer-1 exited with code 3 (restarting)

Cause: Images before spieli 0.9.0 applied api.sql on daemon startup before the first import had created the planet_osm_* tables, so the schema apply failed and the container restarted before it ever reached the import. The API_ONLY mode line in the log is misleading — that banner was printed unconditionally; API_ONLY was not actually set.

Fix: Pull a current image and restart:

docker compose pull importer
docker compose --profile <mode> up -d importer

The importer now defers the startup schema apply until an import has completed, and logs No completed import on record — deferring API schema apply to first import. instead.

Workaround for older images — bootstrap once in one-shot mode, which imports before applying the schema, then start the daemon:

docker compose stop importer
docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MIN_DAYS= \
  -e REIMPORT_INTERVAL_MAX_DAYS= \
  importer
docker compose --profile <mode> up -d importer

API_ONLY=1 on a never-imported database

api.sql cannot be applied before the first import. Current images exit with No completed import on record — nothing to apply yet. instead of failing inside api.sql, so the API_ONLY=1 step of a sequential upgrade sweep (scripts/upgrade-stacks.sh) is no longer aborted by a stack that has never imported. The get_meta verification that follows also no longer aborts the sweep: such a stack has no api schema, so get_meta answers 404, which the script reports as "most likely never completed an import" and records rather than treating as fatal. The remaining stacks are still upgraded, and the sweep exits non-zero at the end with the list of stacks whose verification was inconclusive.

docs.title: Map loads but shows no playgrounds
docs.text:
Symptom: Map tiles appear (streets and buildings visible) but no playground polygons are drawn, or the detail panel is empty.

Possible causes:

  1. Import not run or still running — With automatic updates (daemon mode) the importer starts the first import by itself; follow it with docker compose logs -f importer. Without them, run it once: 
    docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm importer
  2. Wrong relation ID — Check OSM_RELATION_ID in .env. The importer uses it to cut your region out of the extract, and get_meta uses it for the region's name and bounding box, so a wrong ID shows up as a missing or wrong name in get_meta, or as playgrounds from a different area. For a state you can check which boundary is in the database (the relation ID with a minus sign): 
    docker compose exec -u postgres db psql -U osm osm \
  -c "SELECT osm_id, name FROM planet_osm_polygon WHERE boundary='administrative' AND admin_level='4';"
    Several commonly cited IDs for German states are off; confirmed values: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern 28322, Sachsen-Anhalt 62607, Schleswig-Holstein 51529. Verify at nominatim.openstreetmap.org, fix .env, then run a full import (Refresh Data) — the data was cut out with the wrong area.
  3. PBF doesn't cover the relation — The PBF extract must geographically contain the relation. If OSM_RELATION_ID is a large region (e.g. a whole state), the PBF_URL must point to a matching extract — a district or city PBF will silently produce 0 playgrounds. Check download.geofabrik.de for the right extract.
  4. Docker stack not running — The app requires a live PostgREST backend. Confirm the stack is running and healthy (docker compose ps).
  5. Browser cache — Try a hard reload: Ctrl+Shift+R (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+R (Mac).
  6. Corrupt PBF cache — get_meta reports playground_count: 0 although the import logged success. A file left broken by an interrupted run is reused, because the importer checks timestamps, not content. Clear the PBF cache and import again.
  7. Right after an upgrade — on v0.9.0 and earlier a failed schema apply could leave playground_stats broken. Run a full import (Refresh Data); see also A stack serves the old schema after an upgrade.

docs.title: Geolocation button does nothing on mobile
docs.text:
Symptom: Tapping the location button on a phone browser has no effect — no movement, no error.

Cause: Browsers block the geolocation API on plain HTTP connections (including local IPs like http://192.168.1.42:8080). This is a browser security policy and cannot be overridden in the app.

Fix options:

  • Test geolocation on the production HTTPS URL.
  • On Android with Chrome: go to chrome://flags, search for "Insecure origins treated as secure", add your local URL, and relaunch Chrome.
  • DuckDuckGo and Brave do not offer this workaround — use Chrome for local geolocation testing.

docs.title: PostgREST returns 404 or connection refused on /api/
docs.text:
Symptom: The app loads but every API call fails with "Failed to fetch" or the network tab shows 502/404 on /api/rpc/*.

Possible causes:

  1. PostgREST container not running — Check docker compose ps. The postgrest service should be running and healthy.
  2. Database not ready — PostgREST starts before PostgreSQL finishes initialising on first launch. It retries automatically, but a docker compose restart postgrest usually resolves it.
  3. Schema cache stale — After applying schema changes, PostgREST needs a schema reload. The importer sends NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload schema' automatically, but if that notification was missed, restart PostgREST: docker compose restart postgrest.
  4. web_anon role missing — db/init.sql creates this role, and the database image runs it only when it finds an empty pgdata volume. If the role is missing anyway, db/init.sql was not mounted when the volume was created — see Add a Data-node → Why copy db/init.sql?. Put the file in place, then recreate the volume, or run it once by hand with psql.

docs.title: Import fails partway through with a PBF error
docs.text:
Symptom: The importer exits with osmium or osm2pgsql reporting a corrupt or truncated file.

Fix: The cached PBF may be corrupt (interrupted download). Delete the cached files and re-run:

docker compose run --rm importer sh -c "rm -f /data/*.pbf"
docker compose --profile data-node-ui run --rm importer

The importer validates the source PBF with osmium fileinfo before using it and will re-download a corrupt file automatically. If the re-download fails, check PBF_URL in .env — make sure the URL is reachable and returns a valid PBF.

docs.title: Hub shows all backends as red / unreachable
docs.text:
Symptom: The instance drawer shows every data-node with a red indicator.

Possible causes:

  1. CORS not configured — The Hub's browser must be able to reach each data-node's /api/ cross-origin over HTTPS. Verify with: 
    curl -I https://your-data-node.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta
# must include: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
  2. registry.json not updated — The Hub still has the bundled dev registry.json pointing at /api and /api2. See Federated Deployment for how to replace it.
  3. Data-node not reachable from browser — The Hub serves the app; the Hub's browser must reach each data-node, not the Hub host. Test from a browser (not the server) by opening each data-node's https://…/api/rpc/get_meta URL directly.
  4. Hub cron not running — Check federation-status.json: if generated_at is older than 5 minutes, the cron job inside the hub container has stopped. Restart the hub container: docker compose --profile ui restart app.

docs.title: Hub shows a backend as reachable but with 0 playgrounds
docs.text:
Symptom: A data-node appears in the Hub instance drawer with a green or yellow indicator, but its playground count is 0 and no playgrounds are drawn from that backend.

Hub operator — diagnose remotely:

curl https://the-data-node.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta

If playground_count is 0 and bbox is [null,null,null,null], the database has no playground data. Pass the findings to the data-node operator.

If playground_count is > 0 and bbox contains real coordinates, the data-node is healthy and the hub has stale cached state — see the next step.

Hub operator — stale cached state (playground_count > 0, valid bbox):

The hub polls each backend's get_meta at startup and every 5 minutes. If the last poll hit the backend while it was mid-import, restarting, or transiently unreachable, the hub cached bbox: null and playgroundCount: 0. With bbox: null the hub's viewport router silently excludes the backend from every map query.

  1. Reload the hub page in the browser. This triggers an immediate re-poll of every backend's get_meta. If playgrounds appear after reload, the cache was stale and self-healed.

  2. Check whether the hub health poller marked the backend down. The hub container runs a 60-second cron that writes federation-status.json; backends that exceed the 3-second curl timeout are marked up: false and the hub orchestrator skips them even when get_meta succeeds from the browser:

curl https://your-hub.example.com/federation-status.json \
  | jq '.backends | to_entries[] | select(.value.up == false) | .key'

If the backend slug appears, it is being skipped by the orchestrator. Check whether the backend is slow to respond:

curl -w '%{time_total}s\n' -o /dev/null -sf \
  https://the-data-node.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta

Response times consistently above 3 seconds will flip up: false on the next hub poll cycle. Investigate slow PostgREST response times on the data-node side (see Map loads but shows no playgrounds for database health checks). If the latency is transient, the hub recovers by itself once the backend is fast again: the cron rewrites the status every 60 seconds, and browsers re-read it every HUB_POLL_INTERVAL (default 300 s). If the hub container is stuck showing a backend as down despite it being healthy, restart it:

docker compose restart app   # run on the hub host

Data-node operator — possible causes:

  1. Import not run — The stack started but no import has completed. With automatic updates, follow it with docker compose logs -f importer; otherwise run it once (Refresh Data).
  2. PBF doesn't cover the relation — See Map loads but shows no playgrounds, cause 3.
  3. Outdated image — See Hub backend returns "function not found" errors.
  4. Daemon importer sleeping after a failed/corrupt previous run — If the importer ran but was OOM-killed during preprocessing, osm2pgsql may have ingested a partial file and recorded a successful last_import_at. The daemon will not retry until the next scheduled interval. Clear the PBF cache, then force a re-import (Daemon mode).

docs.title: Backend shows "No position set" in instance drawer
docs.text:
Symptom: The Hub instance drawer auto-opens and a backend shows a warning: "No position set" with a link to troubleshooting docs.

Cause: The backend entry in registry.json has neither a centroid field nor a valid bbox from its get_meta response. Without position data, the backend cannot be placed on the macro view map.

Fix: Add a centroid field to the backend's entry in registry.json:

{
  "instances": [
    {
      "slug": "your-region",
      "url": "https://your-backend.example.com/api",
      "name": "Your Region",
      "centroid": [10.5, 51.2]
    }
  ]
}

The centroid should be the approximate geographic center of the region in WGS84 coordinates [lon, lat]. Once the first import completes, the bbox from get_meta takes over and the centroid is only used as a fallback.

See also: registry.json Reference for the full schema.

docs.title: Hub backend returns "function not found" errors
docs.text:
Symptom: The hub operator checks the data-node API and gets:

{"code":"PGRST202","message":"Could not find the function api.get_playgrounds_bbox(bbox) in the schema cache."}

The Hub shows 0 playgrounds for that backend.

Hub operator — diagnose remotely:

curl https://the-data-node.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta
# check "version" — if older than v0.4.9, the image needs updating

Data-node operator — fix:

The image predates the tiered-fetch functions added in v0.4.9. Update and re-import, replacing <mode> with the stack's DEPLOY_MODE:

cd ~/spieli   # or wherever spieli was installed
docker compose pull
docker compose --profile <mode> down
docker compose --profile <mode> up -d

Then run a full import as in Refresh Data (the daemon form if automatic updates are on).

Hub operator — verify after the data-node operator confirms the update:

curl https://the-data-node.example.com/api/rpc/get_meta
# playground_count should now be > 0

docs.title: Importer fails with "permission denied" on schema apply
docs.text:
Symptom: psql reports permission denied when the importer runs api.sql.

Cause: The SQL runs as the database user configured in .env. This user needs SUPERUSER or at minimum pg_signal_backend (to terminate PostgREST connections) and CREATE on the public schema. The default user (osm) is a superuser — if you changed POSTGRES_USER, verify the role has these privileges.

Fix:

docker compose -f compose.yml exec db psql -U osm osm
# in psql:
ALTER ROLE your_user SUPERUSER;
\q

Then re-run the importer:

docker compose -f compose.yml --profile <mode> run --rm importer

docs.title: Database volume is very large after repeated imports
docs.text:
Symptom: The pgdata Docker volume grows beyond expectations over time.

Not the cause: playground_stats. Every apply builds it under a staging name and drops the old one, and dropping a relation returns its files to the filesystem at once; there is nothing for VACUUM to reclaim there.

Find out what is large:

docker compose exec db psql -U osm osm -c "
  SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS size
  FROM pg_class WHERE relkind IN ('r','m')
  ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC LIMIT 10;"

The planet_osm_* tables are replaced by every full import. If the total is far above the sizes in Sizing, recreating the data volume and importing once is the quickest clean state.

docs.title: Hub drawer shows "updating" badge that never clears
docs.text:
Symptom: One or more backends in the Hub instance drawer permanently show an "updating" badge, even though no import is running.

Cause: The importing flag in api.import_status was left true by an importer that was killed with SIGKILL (bypasses the EXIT trap) or crashed before the trap could fire.

Self-healing: The importer clears the flag automatically at startup. Restarting the container is usually enough:

docker compose restart importer   # the daemon clears the flag on startup

Manual fix (if you need it cleared immediately without waiting for a restart):

# From the data-node host
docker compose exec db psql -U osm -d osm \
  -c "UPDATE api.import_status SET importing = false WHERE id = 1;"

The Hub picks up the corrected value within a few minutes: the cron rewrites the status every 60 seconds, browsers re-read it every HUB_POLL_INTERVAL.

docs.title: Legal pages missing or showing wrong contact details
docs.text:
Symptom: /legal/impressum or /legal/datenschutz shows stale contact information after updating IMPRESSUM_* vars, or returns 404 (the page is not generated while IMPRESSUM_URL / PRIVACY_URL is set — the app then links that URL instead).

Cause: The HTML files are generated by docker-entrypoint.sh when the app container starts, from the environment it was created with.

Fix: Recreate the app container (restart would keep the old environment):

docker compose --profile <mode> up -d app

If get_meta() still returns the old impressum_url / privacy_url, those are baked in when api.sql is applied. Recreate the daemon importer (up -d importer, it applies a changed api.sql on startup) or run run --rm -e API_ONLY=1 importer. The legal text a hub shows for a data-node is rewritten only by a full import. Details: Configure the instance → Applying legal changes.

Symptom: /legal/impressum says the operator's details have not been configured yet, although IMPRESSUM_NAME is set.

Cause: IMPRESSUM_ADDRESS is also required; without it the entrypoint writes the placeholder page. The Datenschutz page likewise needs IMPRESSUM_NAME and IMPRESSUM_EMAIL.

Fix: Set them in .env, then recreate the app container as above. Which variable each page needs: Configure the instance → Legal pages.

Symptom: PostgREST logs relation "public.playground_stats" does not exist after an upgrade: see Schema apply fails at the top of this page.

docs.title: The map renders, but labels or icons are missing — or the container refuses to start with style.local.json is missing from the image
docs.text: Both come from building an image yourself: the published images carry the vendored fonts and the generated style. See Customise your own image → Build problems. On a published image, report it as a bug.

docs.title: Basemap tiles are slow or fail after an upgrade
docs.text:
Symptom: the map is sluggish or patchy for a while after an upgrade or a container rebuild, then recovers.

Cause: the tile cache lives at /var/cache/nginx/basemap. Without a volume it sits on the container's writable layer and is discarded on every rebuild, so the next visitors refill it from the upstream one tile at a time.

Fix: mount a volume so it survives rebuilds. Both compose.yml and compose.prod.yml ship one (basemap_cache); if you deploy from a hand-written or older compose file, add the equivalent:

services:
  app:
    volumes:
      - basemap_cache:/var/cache/nginx/basemap
volumes:
  basemap_cache:

This matters most for an upgrade sweep across several stacks, which would otherwise send every one of them at the public tile server cold at the same time.

docs.title: Photos, search or reviews stopped working after an upgrade
docs.text:
These features are served through /ext/ paths on your own instance rather than fetched from the third party by the browser. Three things go wrong quietly.

A cold cache after a rebuild. Recreating the container (an upgrade, up -d after a config change) replaces it, and a cache on the writable layer goes with it. compose.yml mounts a named volume (ext_cache) so this should not happen — check it is actually mounted:

docker compose exec app du -sh /var/cache/nginx/ext
docker compose config | grep -A2 ext_cache

Search returns nothing under load. The Nominatim proxy shares the OSMF limit of 1 request per second across the whole instance, and sheds beyond it rather than exceeding the policy. Cached queries are unaffected — the limiter only sees misses — so this shows up as unusual free-text searches failing while region URLs keep working. Look for limiting requests in the error log (the error log is the only one there is, #988; it holds the shed request line, so treat it with care):

docker compose logs app | grep "limiting requests"

If you see it routinely, PROXY_NOMINATIM=false sends each visitor's searches to the public Nominatim directly, so the limit applies per visitor instead of to your server, at the cost of that privacy property. There is no setting to point spieli at a Nominatim of your own; the upstream is fixed.

Images render as broken. Check whether the request 404s at your instance or at Wikimedia:

docker compose logs app | grep -i "ext/wikimedia"

No request is access-logged (#988), /ext/ included, so a successful request leaves no trace by design — only errors appear. A 404 from the instance itself means the path did not match the allowlist; the most likely cause is Wikimedia serving files from a host the proxy does not know about. The proxy accepts any *.wikimedia.org host, so this should be rare, but it is the first thing to check if thumbnails break after a Wikimedia change.

To rule the proxies out entirely, set PROXY_COMMONS=false and restart: the browser then fetches from Wikimedia directly, as it did before.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text: Steps to completely remove a spieli deployment from a server.

docs.title: 1. Remove the Traefik stack
docs.text:
If you set up the Traefik reverse proxy:

cd spieli-traefik

# Stop containers and delete certificate volumes
docker compose down -v

cd ..
rm -rf spieli-traefik/ install-traefik.sh

docs.title: 2. Remove the spieli stack
docs.text:
cd spieli

# Stop all containers (all profiles), delete volumes and networks
docker compose down -v --remove-orphans

cd ..
rm -rf spieli/ install.sh

No --profile flag needed — down stops all containers in the project regardless of which profile started them (including watchtower if auto-update was enabled). --remove-orphans also removes containers of services that are no longer in compose.yml.

If a volume removal fails with "volume is in use", a stopped container is still referencing it. Prune stopped containers first, then remove the volumes manually:

docker container prune -f
# the prefix is the compose project name; `docker volume ls` shows the exact names
docker volume rm spieli_pgdata spieli_pbf_cache spieli_basemap_cache spieli_ext_cache 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: 3. Remove Docker images (optional)
docs.text:
docker image prune -a

This removes all unused images

docker image prune -a removes every image not referenced by a running container — not just spieli images. Skip this step if other Docker workloads are running on the same host.

docs.title: Before you upgrade
docs.text:
Check GitHub Releases for the latest version and scan the release notes for breaking labels. Most releases carry none and require no manual action.

Label What it means What you must do requires-env-update New or removed env var Update .env before pulling the new image requires-compose-update compose.yml changed structurally Re-run install.sh or update compose.yml manually before restarting requires-reimport OSM data model changed Trigger a full re-import after the image update lands requires-schema-update api.sql changed With Watchtower: nothing, the daemon applies it on restart. Manual upgrade: steps 2–4 below

No database backup needed. Everything in the database comes from OpenStreetMap; if an upgrade goes wrong, a re-import rebuilds it. What cannot be rebuilt is your .env (and on a hub, registry.json) — keep a copy of those. Details: Backup and Restore.

To check what version is currently running:

docker inspect spieli-app-1 --format '{{index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version"}}'
# or
docker compose images

docs.title: Automatic upgrade (Watchtower)
docs.text:
The installer's "automatic updates" answer turns on the auto-update profile, which runs Watchtower. To enable it by hand, add the profile to your up command:

docker compose --profile <mode> --profile auto-update up -d

Watchtower checks the image registry (GHCR) once every 24 hours. When a new image is published it pulls it, restarts app and importer, and removes the replaced image:

  • The daemon importer applies a changed api.sql when its container starts, so schema changes take effect right after the restart — no separate API_ONLY=1 step needed. An unchanged api.sql is skipped (#971).
  • The importer's startup grace check prevents an unplanned re-import: if a recent import is on record, it goes back to sleep (Scheduled Import → What happens on container startup).

Standard releases (no breaking labels): nothing to do. A new release reaches your stack within a day.

For breaking-label releases, follow the Breaking label procedures below in addition to the Watchtower restart. Subscribe to GitHub Releases so you notice them.

One Watchtower per host

Watchtower watches every container on the Docker host, not only its own stack. With several stacks on one host, only one of them (by convention the hub) runs --profile auto-update; a second Watchtower would fight the first over the same containers. The data-node stacks are still updated, without the profile.

docs.title: Manual upgrade
docs.text: Use manual steps when you don't run Watchtower, or when a breaking label requires a specific action sequence.

docs.title: Hub (DEPLOY_MODE=ui)
docs.text:
The hub has no database and no importer — only the app container needs updating.

cd /path/to/your/spieli-hub

docker compose pull
docker compose --profile ui up -d app

Done. No API_ONLY=1, no importer, no verify step needed.

docs.title: Standalone or Data-node (DEPLOY_MODE=data-node-ui or data-node)
docs.text:
Replace <mode> with your DEPLOY_MODE and <port> with your APP_PORT.

Step 1 — Pull new images

docker compose pull

Step 2 — Stop the daemon importer

docker compose --profile <mode> stop importer

This is not optional, and it is not the same as "the daemon is idle". The daemon applies api.sql on container startup, so anything that restarts it — a reboot, Watchtower, up -d — makes it a second writer against the same schema. Stopping it removes that possibility for the duration of the apply.

Step 3 — Apply schema changes (API_ONLY)

docker compose --profile <mode> run --rm -e API_ONLY=1 importer

This updates all PostgREST functions and the version number reported by get_meta. It runs as a one-shot container, and with the daemon stopped it is the only writer.

Concurrent applies queue rather than race

api.sql takes a session-level advisory lock, so if something applies the schema at the same time — a manual make db-apply, a Watchtower-triggered restart — the second one waits instead of corrupting the first.

That is a safety net, not a substitute for step 2. The last writer still wins, and the lock cannot tell an old image from a new one: if the daemon on its previous image applies last, the stack ends up serving the old schema while reporting healthy. Stopping it first is what prevents that.

If API_ONLY=1 fails mid-run

Since v0.10.0 the API stays up: playground_stats is built under a staging name and swapped in, so a crash before the swap leaves the previous view serving traffic. Re-run API_ONLY=1 after fixing the cause — the staging view is dropped and rebuilt on the next attempt. On v0.9.0 and earlier the view was dropped first, and a crash partway through left it gone, with PostgREST logging relation "public.playground_stats" does not exist; recovery there is a full re-import.

Step 4 — Recreate the daemon importer on the new image

docker compose --profile <mode> up -d --force-recreate importer

--force-recreate matters. A plain up -d importer restarts the existing container, which leaves the daemon on the old image — and since its startup path applies api.sql, the old image then becomes the last writer and quietly restores the old schema. That is what happened during the v0.9.0 sweep (#800): the stack ran the new app against the old schema, with two filters silently wrong while get_meta and row counts looked healthy.

What the recreated daemon does on startup

It compares the api.sql it would apply with the one step 3 just applied. They match, so it skips the apply and logs api.sql and the live schema unchanged since the last completed apply — skipping the startup apply (#971). If it logs Applying API schema on startup instead, it rebuilds playground_stats, which takes minutes on a large region. The API keeps serving meanwhile, from the previous view, which is swapped out only at the end. Either way, check the log before verifying:

docker compose --profile <mode> logs -f importer

Step 5 — Restart the app container

docker compose --profile <mode> up -d app

Step 6 — Verify

curl -sf http://localhost:<port>/api/rpc/get_meta | \
